[chapter 1]

## Chapter I

[section 1]

## General View of the Moods.

§1

The Mood of a verb shows the manner in which the assertion of the verb is made.

The Greek verb has four moods, properly so called,—the
indicative, the subjunctive, the optative, and the imperative. The
infinitive, which is a verbal noun, and the participle and the verbal in
-te/os, which are
verbal adjectives, are so closely connected with the moods in many
constructions, that they are discussed with them in Syntax.

The four proper moods, as opposed to the infinitive, are
sometimes called the finite moods. The
subjunctive, optative, imperative, and infinitive, as opposed to the
indicative, are sometimes called the dependent moods.

[section 2]

## I. Indicative.

§2

The indicative, in its most primitive use, makes a simple,
absolute assertion, or asks a question which includes or concerns such
an assertion. e.g. *gra/fei,
he is writing;
e)/grafen, he was writing;
e)/grayen, he wrote;
gra/yei, he will write.
*gra/fei;, is he writing?
e)gra/yate;, did you write?
gra/yete;, will you write?
ti/ e)/grayen;, what did he write?

§3

The indicative may also express

(a)

A dependent statement (or quotation) of such an
absolute assertion or question. e.g., *le/gei o(/ti gra/fei, he says that he is writing (he says
gra/fw); le/gei o(/ti gra/yei,
he says that he will write
(he says gra/yw);
e)rwta=| ti/
e)gra/yamen, he asks what we
wrote; e)rwta=|
ei) e)/graya, he asks whether
I wrote.
(b)

A distinct statement of an object aimed at or
feared. e.g., *)epimelei=tai
o(/pws tou=to genh/setai, he
takes care that this shall be done
(339);
fobou/meqa mh\
a)mfote/rwn h(marth/kamen, we
fear that we have missed both (369, 2).
(c)

A distinct supposition of an absolute
statement, that is, a supposition that such a statement is, was,
or will be true. E.g., *ei)
gra/fei, if he is writing;
ei) e)/grayen,
if he wrote;
ei) ge/grafe, if he has written;
ei) gra/yei, if he shall write or if he is to write. What is supposed in
each case could be expressed by gra/fei, e)/grayen, ge/grafe, or
gra/yei.

§4

The past tenses of the indicative may, further, express a
supposition that some statement either had
been or were now true, while it is
implied that really it was not or is not true. E.g.

*ei) e)/graya,
if I had written;
ei) e)/grafon, if I were now writing or if I had been writing; the context indicating
that really I did not write or am not writing
(410). These
expressions originally always referred to the past, as they do in
Homer.

§5

Out of the form of unreal supposition (4) were developed after Homer the
use of the past tenses of the indicative with ei)/qe or ei) ga/r in wishes (732); and also the Attic
construction of the past tenses of the indicative to express an
unaccomplished purpose (333), where there is an assimilation of the final clause to
a preceding indicative. E.g. *ei)
ga\r tou=to e)poi/hsa, O if I had
only done this!
*ei)/qe tou=to ei)=xes,
O if you only had this!

*ei)/qe to/t' a)pe/qanon,
i(/na mh\ tou=to e)/paqon, would that
I had then perished, that I might not
have suffered this.

For the indicative with a)/n or ke/,
the potential indicative, see 243.

[section 3]

## II. Subjunctive.

§6

(a)

The subjunctive, in its simplest and apparently
most primitive use, seen in Homer (284), expresses futurity, like the future
indicative, and has ou)
for its negative. E.g.,

*ou) ga/r pw toi/ous
i)/don a)ne/ras ou)de\ i)/dwmai,

for never did I see such men nor
shall I ever see them,

Il. i. 262
;

kai/ pote/ tis
ei)/ph|sin,

and some one will some time say,

Il. vi. 459.

(b)

Though this primitive use disappears in the later
language, the subjunctive still remains closely related in sense to
the future indicative, and in most of its constructions can be
interchanged with it.

§7

The subjunctive in questions of appeal as to the future (287) has, even in
Homer, developed the idea of propriety or expediency. E.g.

*au)=qi me/nw h)=e qe/w;

shall I remain here or run?

Il. x.
62.
So

ph=| i)/w;

whither shall I go?

Od. xv.
509.
But the future indicative can be used in the same sense; as
ti/ dh=ta drw=men; mhte/r' h)=
foneu/somen;

what are we to do? shall we slay our mother?

EUR. El.
967.（See
68.)

§8

(a)

In exhortations and in prohibitions with mh/ (250, 259) the subjunctive has an
imperative force, and is always future; as in i)/wmen, let us
go;
mh\ qauma/shte, do not wonder.

The future indicative occasionally occurs in
prohibitions with mh/
(70).

(b)

The subjunctive with mh/, especially in Homer, may express a
future object of fear with a desire to avert it; as in mh\ nh=as e(/lwsi, may they not seize the ships (as I fear they
will). (See 261.) From such expressions combined with verbs of
fearing arose the dependent use of mh/ with the subjunctive expressing a
future object of fear; as fobou=mai mh\ a)po/lhtai, I fear
that he may perish.

§9

In the constructions with ou) mh/
(294) the
subjunctive and the future indicative are used, without apparent
distinction, in a future sense; as ou) mh\ ge/nhtai and ou) mh\ genh/setai, it will not happen.

§10

The subjunctive may express a future purpose or a future
object of care or exertion. E.g. *)/erxetai o(/pws tou=to i)/dh|, he
comes that he may see this
(317); e)pimelei=tai o(/pws tou=to
ge/nhtai (or genh/setai), he takes care that this shall
be done
(339). In clauses
of purpose the future indicative is sometimes used (324), and in the construction of
339 it became the regular Attic form.

§11

In conditional clauses the subjunctive expresses either a
future supposition (444), or a general supposition which is indefinite (never
strictly present) in its time (462).

(a)

In the former it supposes such a future case as
the Homeric subjunctive (6) states; as e)a/n tis ei)/ph|, if one shall say (the thing supposed
being ei)/ph| tis,
one will say); here the
future indicative may be used in essentially the same sense (447). In
the general condition it supposes an event to occur at any time,
as we say if any one ever goes or
whoever goes, with an apodosis
expressing repetition or a general truth; as e)a/n tis kle/yh| (or o(\s a)\n kle/yh|),
kola/zetai,
if any one steals [note: (or whoever
steals)] , he is always punished.
(b)

The subjunctive in general suppositions is the
only subjunctive which does not refer to future time, and here
the future indicative can never be used. In most other languages
(as in English and generally in Latin), and sometimes in Greek,
such a condition is expressed by the present indicative, like an
ordinary present supposition; but the Greek, in its desire to
avoid a form denoting present time, generally fell into one
which it uses elsewhere only for future time. The construction,
however, appears in Homer imperfectly established, except in
relative clauses (468): this indicates that it does not belong to the
primitive uses of the subjunctive. (See 17.)

For the Homeric subjunctive with ke/ or a)/n in independent sentences, which does not differ
perceptibly in meaning from the future with ke/ or a)/n, see
201, 1.

[section 4]

## III. Optative.

§12

The optative is commonly a less distinct and direct form of
expression than the subjunctive, imperative, or indicative, in
constructions of the same general character as those in which these
moods are used.

§13

This is seen especially in independent sentences, where the
optative either expresses a wish or exhortation, or is used (regularly
with a)/n or ke/) in a potential sense.

Thus i)/oimen,
may we go, corresponds as a weaker
form to i)/wmen, let us go. Corresponding to e)celqw/n tis i)de/tw, let some one go out and see, we have

e)celqw/n tis i)/doi,

may some one go out and see,

Od. xxiv.
491
. *(/eloito a)/n,
he would take or he might take, corresponds to the Homeric e(/lhtai or e(/lhtai/ ke, he will
take or he may take (201, 1).

We find in Homer a few optatives expressing concession or
permission, which have a neutral sense and can hardly be classed as
either potential or wishing. See

Il. iv. 17,

ei) d' au)= pws to/de pa=si
fi/lon kai\ h(du\ pe/loito, h)= toi me\n oi)ke/oito po/lis
*pria/moio a)/naktos, au)=tis d' *)argei/hn *(ele/nhn *mene/laos
a)/goito
, where we may translate the apodosis either let the city still be a habitation and let M. carry
away Helen, or the city may still be
a habitation and M. may carry away Helen. In
iii. 72 we have
gunai=ka/ te oi)/kad'
a)ge/sqw, and in
iii. 255
tw=| de/ ke nikh/santi gunh\ kai\
kth/maq' e(/poito, where a)ge/sqw and e(/poito/
ke refer to essentially the same thing with a)/goito in
iv. 19.
Following
Il. iii.
255(above) we have oi( d'
a)/lloi nai/oimen *troi/hn, toi\ de\ ne/ontai, i. e. the rest of us may remain dwellers in Troy, while
they will return to Greece. From such neutral future
expressions were probably developed the two distinct uses of the
optative. In its hortatory sense as a form of wishing, the optative was
distinguished by the use of mh/ as a negative; while in its potential sense it had ou) as its negative (as in
ou) mh\n ga/r ti kakw/teron
a)/llo pa/qoimi, for really I can
suffer nothing worse,
Il. xix. 321), and it was soon
further marked by the addition of ke/ or a)/n.
(See Appendix I.)

§14

In dependent clauses expressing purpose or the object of
exertion or of fear, the optative is never an original form; but it
always represents a dependent subjunctive or future indicative (8, b; 10) in the changed
relation in which either of them is placed when its leading verb is
changed from present or future to past time.

We represent this change in English by a change from may to might, or
from shall or will to should or would; as e)/rxetai i(/na i)/dh|, he comes
that he may see, h)=lqen
i(/na i)/doi, he came that he might
see;
e)pimelei=tai o(/pws tou=to
genh/setai, he takes care that this
shall be done, e)pemelei=to o(/pws tou=to genh/soito, he took care that this should be done;
fobei=tai mh\ tou=to pa/qh|,
he fears that he may suffer this;
e)fobh/qh mh\ tou=to pa/qoi,
he feared that he might suffer this.
Here the original subjunctive or future indicative (especially the
latter) is very often used in place of the optative.

§15

In all forms of indirect discourse the same principle (14) holds, that the
optative after past tenses represents (in a changed relation) an
indicative or a subjunctive of the direct form, which original mood is
always used after present and future tenses, and may be retained after
past tenses (667,
1).

Here again we see what the change is, for we represent it by
our change from is to was, have to had, shall and
will to should and would, etc.; as le/gei o(/ti a)lhqe/s e)stin,
he says that it is true;
e)/lecen o(/ti a)lhqe\s
ei)/h (or e)sti/n),
he said that it was true;
le/gei o(/ti gra/yei, he says that he will write;
e)/lecen o(/ti gra/yoi (or
gra/yei), he said that he would write. So ou)k oi)=da ti/ ei)/pw, I know not what I shall say;
ou)k h)/|dein ti/ ei)/poimi
(or ei)/pw), I knew not what I should say.

§16

In future conditions the optative expresses the supposition
in a weakened future form, as compared with the stronger future of the
subjunctive and the future indicative.

Compare e)a\n
e)/lqw, if I (shall) go
(444), with ei) e)/lqoimi, if I should go
(455). Often the
form of the leading sentence (the apodosis) decides whether a given
supposition shall be expressed by a subjunctive or by an optative; thus
in
DEM. iv. 11
we have a)\n ou(=to/s ti
pa/qh|, if anything happens (shall
happen) to him (Philip), depending on poih/sete; and in the next sentence,
referring to precisely the same contingency, we have ei)/ ti pa/qoi, depending on two optatives
with a)/n.

§17

The only remaining form of dependent optative is that found
in past general suppositions, as ei)/ tis kle/yeien (or o(\s kle/yeien), e)kola/zeto, if ever any one
stole (or whoever stole), he was (always) punished (462; 531).

Here the optative after a past tense represents an original
subjunctive after a present tense (11), differing in this from the optative in
future conditions (16), which is in an original construction. The late development
of this optative appears from its almost total absence in protasis with
ei) in Homer (468), where the
corresponding subjunctive in protasis is also infrequent. It may
therefore be disregarded in considering the primitive uses of the
optative. (See 11
b.）

For a more full discussion of the relations of the optative
to the other moods, see Appendix I.

[section 5]

## IV. Imperative.

§18

The imperative expresses a command, exhortation, entreaty, or
prohibition (250
and 259). E.g.
*feu=ge, begone!
*)elqe/tw, let him come.
*do/s moi tou=to, give me this.
*mh\ poi/ei a)/dika, do not do what is unjust.

[chapter 2]

## Chapter II

[section 6]

## The Tenses.

§19

There are seven Tenses,—the present, imperfect,
perfect, pluperfect, aorist, future, and future perfect. The imperfect
and pluperfect occur only in the indicative; the futures are wanting in
the subjunctive and imperative.

§20

These tenses may express two relations. They may designate
the time of an action as present, past, or
future; and also its character as going on, finished, or simply taking place. The latter relation is expressed
by the tenses in all the moods and in the infinitive and the participle;
the former is always expressed in the indicative, and to a certain
extent (to be explained below) in the dependent moods and the
participle.

§21

The tenses are divided into primary tenses, which denote present or future time, and secondary or historical tenses, which denote past time. This distinction
applies properly only to the tenses of the indicative; but it may be
extended to any forms of the dependent moods which have the same
distinction of time as the tenses of the indicative.

The primary tenses of the indicative are the present (in its
ordinary uses), perfect, future, and future perfect. The secondary
tenses are the imperfect, pluperfect, and aorist (in its ordinary uses).

This distinction will be more fully explained at the end of
this chapter (165-191). It must be noted that the historic present (33) is a secondary
tense, and the gnomic aorist (154) is a primary tense.

§22

In speaking of the time denoted by any verb, we must
distinguish between time which is present, past, or future with
reference to the time of speaking or writing (that is, time absolutely present, etc.), and time which is
present, past, or future with reference to the time of some verb with
which the verbal form in question is connected (that is, time relatively present, etc.) Thus, when we say
tou=to a)lhqe/s e)stin,
this is true, e)sti/n is present with reference to the
time of speaking; but when we say e)/fh tou=to a)lhqe\s ei)=nai or ei)=pen o(/ti tou=to a)lhqe/s e)stin (or
ei)/h), he said that this was true, (i.e. he said “this is true”), the
present tense which we use denotes time present to the time of the
leading verb, i.e. time absolutely past and
only relatively present. The same
distinction is seen between the future in tou=to genh/setai, this will happen, and that in e)/fh tou=to genh/sesqai or ei)=pen o(/ti genh/setai
(genh/soito), he said that this would happen; where the
future in the first case is absolutely
future, but in the other cases is only relatively future and may be even absolutely past. Again, in tou=to e)ge/neto, this happened, the aorist is absolutely past; but in e)/fh tou=to gene/sqai, or
ei)=pen o(/ti tou=to
e)ge/neto (or ge/noito), he said that this had
happened, it denotes time past to the time of the past
leading verb, and so is doubly past. But in
connection with a future expression an aorist, though relatively past,
may be absolutely future; as in

PLAT. Rep. 478
D,

to\ fane/n
as subject of e)/sesqai means that which will
hereafter have appeared. So diapraca/menos in
496 E. (See 143.)

It is a special distinction between the Greek and the English
idioms, that the Greek uses its verbal forms much more freely to denote
merely relative time. Thus, we translate the Greek presents ei)=nai and e)sti/ after e)/fh or ei)=pen (above) by our was; the
futures genh/sesqai and
genh/setai by would happen; and the aorists gene/sqai and e)ge/neto by had happened. This distinction appears
especially in the indicative, optative, and infinitive of indirect
discourse; in future forms after past tenses in final and object clauses
with i(/na, o(/pws, etc.;
and usually in the participle; but not in protasis.

[section 7]

## I. Tenses of the Indicative: Present.

§23

The present indicative represents an action as going on at the time of speaking or writing;
as gra/fw, I write, or I am
writing.

An important exception occurs when the present indicative in
indirect discourse denotes time which is present relatively to the
leading verb. See above, 22; 669,
2; 674,
1.

§24

As the limits of such an action on either side of the present
moment are not defined, the present may express a customary or repeated action or
a general truth. E.g.

*(h pru/mna tou= ploi/ou
o(\ ei)s *dh=lon *)aqhnai=oi pe/mpousin,

the stern of the ship which the
Athenians send to Delos (every year).

PLAT.
Phaed. 58A.

*ti/ktei toi ko/ros
u(/brin, o(/tan kakw=| o)/lbos e(/phtai,

satiety begets insolence, whenever
prosperity follows the wicked.

THEOG.
153.

*)en xro/nw| a)pofqi/nei
to\ ta/rbos a)nqrw/poisin,

in time timidity dies out in men.

AESCH.
Ag. 857.

§25

The present denotes merely the continuance or progress of an
action, without reference to its completion. It may, however, be implied
by the context that the action is not to be
completed, so that the present denotes an attempted or intended action.
Especially di/dwmi, in the
sense of offer, and pei/qw, try to
persuade, are thus used. E.g.

*nu=n d' a(/ma t'
au)ti/ka polla\ didoi=,

he offers many things.

ix. 519.

e)nanti/a kai\ toi=s no/mois kai\ tw=| dikai/w|

they are trying to persuade you to
vote contrary both to the laws and to justice.

26.

This conative signification is
much more common in the imperfect. See 36 and the examples.

## Imperfect.

§34

The imperfect represents an action as going on in past time; as e)/grafon, I was
writing.

§35

The imperfect is thus a present transferred to the past,
retaining all the peculiarities of the present which are consistent with
the change. Thus it may denote a customary or repeated action, or a
series of actions; or, if it refers to a single action (as it very
frequently does), it represents it in its progress rather than as a
simple past occurrence (like the aorist). In narration it dwells on the
course of an event instead of merely stating its occurrence. E.g.

*)epi\ *ke/kropos h(
*)attikh\ kata\ po/leis w)|kei=to, kai\ ou) cunh/|esan
bouleuso/menoi, a)ll' au)toi\ e(/kastoi e)politeu/onto

e)basi/leusen, e)s th\n nu=n po/lin ou)=san cunw/|kise
pa/ntas.

## Perfect and Pluperfect.

§42

The perfect represents an action as already finished at the
present time; as ge/grafa, I have
written (that is, my writing is now
finished).

§43

The pluperfect represents an action as already finished at a
given past time; as e)gegra/fein, I had
written (that is, my writing was
finished at some specified past time).

§44

The perfect, although it implies the performance of the
action in past time, yet states only that it stands
completed at the present time.
This explains why the perfect is classed with the present as a primary
tense, that is, as a tense of present
time.

§45

The perfect and the pluperfect may be expressed by the
perfect participle with the present and imperfect of ei)mi/. Here, however, each part of the
compound generally retains its own signification, so that this form
expresses more fully the continuance of the result of the action of the perfect to the present time, and of that of the pluperfect to the past time referred to. E.g.

*pepoihkw/s
e)stin (or h)=n), he is (or was) in the
condition of having done,—he has done (or had done).

*)emou= oi( no/moi ou)
mo/non a)pegnwko/tes ei)si\ mh\ a)dikei=n, a)lla\ kai\
kekeleuko/tes tau/thn th\n di/khn lamba/nein,

it is the laws which not only have
acquitted me of injustice, but have commanded me to
inflict this punishment.

LYS. i.
34.

*)eto/lma le/gein w(s
e)gw\ to\ pra=gm' ei)mi\ tou=to dedrakw/s,

who had done this deed.

[section 11]

## Aorist.

§53

The aorist indicative expresses the simple occurrence of an action in past time; as
e)/graya, I wrote.

§54

This fundamental idea of simple
occurrence remains the essential characteristic of the aorist
through all the dependent moods, however indefinite they may be in
regard to time. The aorist takes its name
(a)o/ristos, unlimited, unqualified) from its thus
denoting merely the occurrence of an action, without any of the
limitations (o(/roi) as to
completion, continuance, repetition,
etc., which belong to other tenses. It corresponds to the ordinary
preterite (e.g. did, went, said) in
English, whereas the Greek imperfect corresponds generally to the forms
I was doing, etc. Thus, e)poi/ei tou=to is he was doing this or he did this habitually; pepoi/hke tou=to is he has already
done this; e)pepoih/kei
tou=to is he had already (at some
past time) done this; but e)poi/hse tou=to is simply he did this, without qualification of any
kind.

§55

The aorist of verbs which denote a state or condition generally
expresses the entrance into that state or condition. E.g. *basileu/w, I am king, e)basi/leusa, I
became king;
a)/rxw, I hold office, h)=rca, I took
office;
ploutw=, e)plou/thsa, I became rich.

*th=| a)lhqei/a| sunw/|kei kai\
ou)de/pw kai\ th/meron a)pole/loipen: a)lla\ para\ zw=ntos
*timokra/tous e)kei/nw| sunw/|khse,

she was his wife in good faith, and
has not yet even to this day been divorced; but she went to live
with him from Timocrates while T. was still living.

DEM. XXX.
33.

§56

The aorist is distinguished from the imperfect by expressing
only the occurrence of an action or the entrance into a state or
condition, while the imperfect properly represents an action or state as
going on or as repeated. See the examples of the imperfect and aorist in
35, and compare
sunw/|kei and sunw/|khse in
DEM. xxx. 33
(in 55). The
aorist is therefore more common in rapid narration, the imperfect in
detailed description. It must be remembered that the same event may be
looked upon from different points of view by the same person; thus in

DEM. xviii.
71 and
73
(quoted in 35) e)/lue th\n
ei)rh/nhn and th\n ei)rh/nhn
e)/luse refer to the same thing, once as an act in progress,
and once as a fact accomplished. No amount of duration in an act,
therefore, can make the aorist an improper form to express it, provided
it is stated as a single past event viewed as a whole. Thus e)basi/leuse de/ka e)/th (see

HDT. ii.
157) means he had a reign of ten
years, (which is viewed as a single past event), while e)basi/leue de/ka e)/th might
refer to the same reign in the sense he was
reigning during ten years. The aorist may refer even to a
series of repetitions; but it takes them collectively as a whole, while
the imperfect would take them separately as individuals. See

DEM. xviii. 80,

meta\ tau=ta de\ tou\s
a)posto/lous a(/pantas a)pe/steila
, and afterwards I sent out all the naval
armaments; and

xviii. 60,

a(\ me\n pro\ tou= politeu/esqai
kai\ dhmhgorei=n e)me\ prou)/labe kai\ kate/sxe
*fi/lippos
, the (succession of) advantages which
Philip secured during the period before I entered public
life, emphatically opposed (as a whole) to Philip's many
failures after that time, which are mentioned in a(\ de\ kai\ diekwlu/qh. If the orator had
wished to dwell on the number of the advantages or failures, or on their
duration, he could have used the imperfect. See the last example under
35.

§57

Since the same event may thus be stated by the aorist or the
imperfect according to the writer's point of view, it is natural that it
should occasionally be a matter of indifference which form is used,
especially when the action is of such a nature that it is not important
to distinguish its duration from its occurrence. For example, this
distinction can seldom be important in such expressions as he said, he commanded; and we find e)/legon and e)ke/leuon in the historians
where no idea of duration can have been in mind. See

oi( d' e)ke/leuo/n te e)pie/nai,
kai\ parelqo/ntes oi( *)aqhnai=oi e)/legon toia/de,

THUC. i. 72
, followed, at the end of the speech in
79, by toiau=ta de\ oi( *)aqhnai=oi ei)=pon and
*)arxi/damos e)/lece
toia/de. In such cases as the following (cited with others by
Krüger) it was not important to the narrative whether the idea of
duration was included in the expression or not: ba/lleto and ba/leto,
Il. ii. 43 and
45; qh=ken and ti/qei,
Il. xxiii. 653 and 656; dw=ke and di/dou,
Il. vii. 303 and 305; e)/lipen and lei=pe,
Il. ii. 106
and 107; compare also mi/stullon with e)/peiran,
w)/pthsan, and e)ru/santo,
Il. i. 465 and 466. In all these cases the
fundamental distinction of the tenses, which was inherent in the form,
remained; only it happened that either of the two distinct forms
expressed the meaning which was here needed equally well. It must not be
thought, from these occasional examples, that the Greeks of any period
were not fully alive to the distinction of the two tenses and could not
use it with skill and nicety. But the Greeks, like other workmen, did
not care to use their finest tools on every occasion; and it is often
necessary to remember this if we would avoid hair-splitting.

§58

The aorist, expressing simply a past occurrence, is sometimes

## Future.

§63

The future denotes that an action is to take place in time to
come; as gra/yw, I shall write or I
shall be writing, sometimes I will
write;
pei/setai, he will suffer, sometimes he shall suffer.

§64

In indirect discourse and in all final constructions the
future expresses time future relatively to the leading verb. See 22.

§65

occurrence, or its inception; as e(/cw, I shall have, or
I shall obtain;
tou=to dw/sw, I shall give this;

## Future Perfect.

§77

The future perfect denotes that an action will be already finished at some future time. It is
thus a perfect transferred to the future. E.g.

*kai/ me e)a\n
e)cele/gch|s, ou)k a)xqesqh/somai/ soi, a)lla\ me/gistos
eu)erge/ths par' e)moi\ a)nagegra/yei,

you will have been enrolled as my
greatest benefactor.

PLAT.
Gorg. 506 C

*)\hn de\ mh\ ge/nhtai,
ma/thn e)moi\ keklau/setai, su\ d' e)gxanw\n teqnh/ceis,

I shall then have had my whippings
for nothing, and you will have died grinning.

AR.
Nub. 1435.

§78

The future perfect often denotes the continuance of an
action, or the permanence of its results, in future time. E.g.

*du/namin, h(=s e)s a)i/dion
toi=s e)pigignome/nois mnh/mh katalelei/yetai,

our posterity for ever.

64.
(Compare 105.）

and e)/somai. In the active

de/onta e)so/meqa e)gnwko/tes kai\ lo/gwn matai/wn

(See 45 and

§82

When the perfect is used in the sense of a present (49), the future
perfect is its regular future; as keklh/somai, memnh/somai, a)festh/cw, I shall be named, I shall remember, I shall
withdraw, etc.

§83

In many other verbs, the future perfect differs very
slightly, if at all, from an ordinary future. Thus pepra/somai is the regular future passive of
pipra/skw. Still, where
there is another future, the future perfect is generally more
emphatic.

§84

It must be remembered that, in most cases in which the Latin
or the English would use a future perfect in a dependent clause, the
Greek uses an aorist or even a perfect subjunctive. (See 90 and 103, with the examples.)

[section 14]

## II. Tenses of the Dependent Moods.

§85

The distinctions of time which mark the various tenses in the
indicative are retained when the optative and infinitive represent the
indicative in indirect discourse, and usually in the participle. But in
other constructions these distinctions of time disappear in the
dependent moods, and the tenses here differ only in their other
character of denoting the continuance, the
completion, or simply the occurrence of an action (20). The infinitive with a)/n is not included in this
statement (see Chap. III.)

The tenses in these two uses must, therefore, be discussed
separately.

[section 15]

## Not in Indirect Discourse.

§86

In the subjunctive and imperative, and also in the optative
and infinitive not in indirect discourse (666; 684), the tenses chiefly used are
the present and the aorist. The perfect is used here only when the
completion of the action is to be emphasized (see 102-110). For the occasional
future, see 111-113; 130-132.

[section 16]

## Present and Aorist.

§87

The present and aorist here differ only in this, that the
present expresses an action in its duration,
that is, as going on or repeated, while the aorist expresses simply its occurrence, the time of both tenses being
otherwise precisely the same. E.g.

*)ea\n
poih=| tou=to, if he shall be
doing this, or if he shall do
this (habitually);

e)a\n
poih/sh| tou=to, (simply) if
he shall do this;

ei) poioi/h
tou=to, if he should be doing
this, or if he should do this
(habitually);

ei)
poih/seie tou=to, if he
should do this;

poi/ei
tou=to, do this
(habitually);

poi/hson
tou=to, do this.

*ou(/tw
nikh/saimi/ t' e)gw\ kai\ nomizoi/mhn sofo/s, on this condition may I gain the victory
(aorist) and be considered (present) wise.

AR.
Nub. 520.

*bou/letai tou=to
poiei=n
, he wishes to do this
(habitually);

bou/letai
tou=to poih=sai, (simply) he
wishes to do this.
For other examples see below.

This is a distinction entirely unknown to the Latin, which
has (for example) only one form, si
faciat, corresponding to ei) poioi/h and ei) poih/seien, and only facere to correspond to both poiei=n and poih=sai (as used above).

§88

It is sometimes difficult here, as in the corresponding case
of the imperfect and the aorist indicative (56; 57), to see any decisive reason for preferring
one tense to the other; and it can hardly be doubted that the Greeks
occasionally failed to make use of this, as well as of other fine
distinctions, when either form would express the required sense equally
well, although they always had the distinction ready for use when it was
needed. Compare the present and the aorist subjunctive and optative in
the following examples:—

*)ea\n ga/r ti/ se fanw=
kako\n pepoihkw\s, o(mologw= a)dikei=n: e)a\n me/ntoi
mhde\n fai/nwmai kako\n pepoihkw\s mhde\ boulhqei\s, ou)
kai\ su\ o(mologh/seis mhde\n u(p' e)mou= a)dikei=sqai;

if I shall appear [note: (aorist)] to have done you any wrong, and if
I shall appear [note: (present)] to have done you no
wrong.

XEN. Cyr. v. 5, 13.

*ei) me\n ga\r
prosde/caito *fwke/as summa/xous . . . ei) de\ mh\
prosde/xoito, k.t.l.

DEM. xix.
318.

*ei)/ tines pollw=n
qana/twn h)=san ai)/tioi, （ i(/na ） pa/ntwn
tou/twn dekaplasi/as a)lghdo/nas u(pe\r e(ka/stou
komi/sainto, kai\ au)= ei)/ tines eu)ergesi/as
eu)ergethko/tes ei)=en, （ i(/na ） kata\
tau)ta\ th\n a)ci/an komi/zointo,

if any had caused many deaths, that
they might receive [note: (aorist)] suffering for all
these, tenfold for each; and again, if they had done
kind services to any, that they might in like manner
receive [note: (present)] their due reward.

PLAT.
Rep. 615B.

In the last example, it is obvious that the change from komi/sainto to komi/zointo is connected with
the change from ei) h)=san
to ei) eu)ergethko/tes
ei)=en; but it is questionable whether the latter change is the
cause or the effect, and it is also quite as hard to see the reason for
this change in the protasis, when both conditions are equally general,
as for that in the final clause. Probably no two scholars would agree in
the reasons which they might assign for the use of the tenses in these
examples. It is certain, however, that either present or aorist would
express the meaning equally well in all these cases.

[section 17]

§90

When the aorist subjunctive depends on e)peida/n (or e)pa/n, e)ph/n), after that, it is referred by this meaning of the particle
to time preceding the action of the leading
verb, so that e)peida\n tou=to
i)/dw, h(/cw means after I (shall)
have seen this, I will come; and e)peida\n tou=to i)dw, a)pe/rxomai, after I have seen this, I (always) depart.
In such cases it may be translated by our future perfect when the
leading verb is future, and by our perfect when the leading verb denotes
a general truth and is translated by the present. As the subjunctive
here can never depend upon a verb of simply present time, it can never refer to time absolutely past; and we use the perfect indicative in
translating such an aorist after a verb expressing a general truth,
merely because we use the present in translating the leading verb,
although this is properly not present but general in its time.

In like manner, after e(/ws, pri/n, and other particles signifying until, before that, and even after the
relative pronoun or e)a/n,
the aorist subjunctive may be translated by our future perfect or
perfect, when the context shows that it refers to time preceding that of
the leading verb. E.g.

*xrh\ de\, o(/tan me\n

§91

This use of the aorist subjunctive (90) sometimes seems to approach
very near to that of the perfect subjunctive (103); and we often translate both
by the same tense. But in the perfect, the idea of an action completed at the time referred to is expressed
by the tense of the verb, without aid from
any particle or from the context; in the aorist, the idea of relative
past time can come only from the particle or
the context. (See
103 with examples, and 104.) The Greek often uses the less precise
aorist subjunctive and optative (see 95) where the perfect would be preferred but for
its cumbrous forms; and we sometimes give the aorist more precision than
really belongs to it in itself by translating it as a perfect or future
perfect. (See the last six examples under 90.) The following example
illustrates the distinction between the perfect and aorist
subjunctive:—

*(\on me\n a)\n i)/dh| a)gnw=ta
[note: （
o( ku/wn ）] , xalepai/nei: o(\n d' a)\n gnw/rimon
[note: （
i)/dh| ）] , a)spa/zetai, ka)\n mhde\n pw/pote u(p
au)tou= a)gaqo\n pepo/nqh|,

whomsoever he sees whom he knows, he fawns
upon, even if he has hitherto received no kindness from him.

PLAT. Rep.
376A.
Compare this with e)a\n
a)gaqo/n ti pa/qh| u(po/ tinos, a)spa/zetai, if he ever happens to receive any kindness from any
one, he always fawns upon him; and e)peida\n a)gaqo/n ti pa/qh|, a)spa/zetai,
after he has received any kindness, he always
fawns upon him.

§93

In a few passages of Homer the aorist subjunctive with mh/ seems to express a similar

555.

la/qwntai

inference drawn from the context. As the later language would use a
perfect subjunctive in such cases, these aorists seem to be instances of
an earlier laxity of usage, like the use of a)po/loito/ ke for both would have perished and would perish
(440).

## Optative.

§94

The present and aorist optative in independent sentences (in
wishes and with a)/n), and
in all conditional sentences except past general conditions (462; 532), express future
time, the relation of which to the future expressed by other moods is
explained in 12,
13, and 16. (Some Homeric
present or past unreal conditions and present wishes are exceptions: see
438-441.) In
all final constructions the optative (which is used only after past
tenses) represents the subjunctive after primary tenses, and is future
relatively to the leading verb. E.g. *ei)/qe tou=to ei)/h

## Infinitive.

§96

A present or aorist infinitive (without a)/n) not in indirect discourse is still a
verbal noun so far that it expresses no time except such as is implied
in the context. Thus, when it depends on a verb of wishing or commanding or any
other verb whose natural object is a future action, or when it expresses
purpose, it is future without regard to its tense; as, in bou/lomai nika=n (or nikh=sai), I wish to be victorious (or to gain victory), the infinitive expresses
time only so far as the noun ni/khn would in bou/lomai
ni/khn. Likewise, when the present or aorist infinitive
(without a)/n) has the
article, except in the rare cases in which it stands in indirect
discourse (794), it
has no reference to time in itself; as in to\ gnw=nai e)pisth/mhn labei=n e)stin,
to learn is to obtain knowledge,
where gnw=nai expresses time
only as the noun gnw=sis
would in its place. E.g.

me/nein, it is possible to
remain.

possible to do this.

§97

The distinction between the present and aorist infinitive is
well illustrated by Aristotle, when he says of pleasure,

Nic.
Eth. x. 3. 4

h(sqh=nai me\n ga\r e)/sti
taxe/ws w(/sper o)rgisqh=nai, h(/desqai d' ou)\, ou)de\ pro\s
e(/teron: badi/zein, de\ kai\ au)/cesqai kai\ pa/nta ta\
toiau=ta. metaba/llein me\n ou)=n ei)s th\n h(donh\n taxe/ws
kai\ brade/ws e)/stin, e)nergei=n de\ kat' au)th\n ou)k e)/sti
taxe/ws, le/gw d' h(/desqai
. We may BECOME pleased (h(sqh=nai) quickly, as
we may get angry quickly; but we cannot BE pleased (h(/desqai) quickly,
even as compared with another person, although we can thus walk and
grow and do such things. We may then change into a state of pleasure
quickly or slowly, but we cannot actually enjoy the pleasure, I mean
BE PLEASED (h(/desqai), quickly.

So in
PLAT. Theaet. 155 C, Socrates says, a)/neu tou= gi/gnesqai gene/sqai
a)du/naton (sc. e)me\
e)la/ttw), i.e. without going through
the process of becoming (gi/gnesqai) smaller, it is impossible for me to get
(gene/sqai）
smaller.

Verbs of hoping, expecting,

[section 20]

## Perfect.

§102

As the perfect indicative represents an act as finished at
the present time, so the perfect of any of
the dependent moods properly represents an act as finished at the time (present, past, or future) at which the
present of that mood would represent it as going on.

§103

in the active, and almost always in the passive and middle, by the
perfect participle with w)=
and ei)/hn; and this
combination of a present and a perfect makes the time denoted especially
clear. Where the present would denote future
time, the perfect denotes future-perfect
time. E.g.

I fear lest the lapse of a long time

91）] .

§104

The perfect subjunctive in protasis corresponds exactly to
the Latin future perfect indicative; but the Greek seldom uses this
cumbrous perfect, preferring the less precise aorist (91). The perfect optative, in both
protasis and apodosis, corresponds to the Latin perfect subjunctive; but
it is seldom used, for a similar reason (95).

The perfect optative can hardly be accurately expressed in
English. For when we use the English forms would
have suffered and should have
suffered to translate the perfect optative, these are merely
vaguer expressions for will and shall have suffered. (See the examples above.)
I should have suffered is commonly past
in English, being equivalent to e)/paqon a)/n; but here it is future, and is therefore
liable to be misunderstood. There is no more reference to past time,
however, in the perfect optative with a)/n, than there is in the future perfect
indicative (77) in
such expressions as

ma/thn e)moi\ keklau/setai,

I shall have had my whippings for nothing
[note: (referring to those received in his boyhood)] ,

[section 21]

## Future.

§111

The future is used in the dependent moods only in the
optative and the infinitive, and in these it is never regular except in
indirect discourse and kindred constructions and in the periphrastic
form with me/llw
(73).

For the future optative in indirect discourse see 128-134; for the
future infinitive in indirect discourse see 135 and 136.

§112

In constructions out of indirect discourse the present and
aorist infinitive can always refer to future time if the context
requires it (96), so
that the future infinitive is here rarely needed. Therefore, after verbs
which naturally have a future action as their object but yet do not
introduce indirect discourse,—as those of commanding, wishing, etc. (684),—the present or aorist infinitive
(not the future) is regularly used. Thus the Greek expresses they wish to do this not by bou/lontai tou=to poih/sein,
but by bou/lontai tou=to
poiei=n (or poih=sai). So the infinitive in other future expressions, as
after w(/ste and in its
final sense, is generally present or aorist. (For the single exception
after me/llw, see 73.)

§113

On the other hand, when it was desired to make the reference
to the future especially prominent, the future infinitive could be used
exceptionally in all these cases. Thus we sometimes find the future
after verbs signifying to be able, to wish, to be
unwilling, and the like; sometimes also in a final sense or
with w(/ste and e)f' w(=|te; and sometimes when
the infinitive with the article refers to future time. This use of the
future is a partial adoption of the form of indirect discourse in other
constructions. It was a particularly favourite usage with Thucydides.
E.g.

*)edeh/qhsan de\ kai\
tw=n *megare/wn nausi\ sfa=s cumprope/myein,

they asked the Megareans also to
escort them with ships.

[section 22]

## Optative and Infinitive of Indirect Discourse.

§115

When the optative and infinitive are in indirect discourse,
each tense represents the corresponding
tense of the direct discourse; the present including also the
imperfect, and the perfect also the pluperfect.

See the general principles of indirect discourse (667). The optative
is included here only as it is used after past tenses to represent an
indicative or subjunctive of the direct discourse. No cases of the
optative or infinitive with a)/n are considered here: for these see Chapter III. For the
meaning of the term
indirect discourse as applied to the
infinitive, see
684.

[section 23]

§120

This use of the present infinitive as an imperfect must be
carefully distinguished from its ordinary use after past tenses, where
we translate it by the imperfect, as in e)/fh to\ stra/teuma ma/xesqai, he said that the army was fighting. This has
sometimes been called an imperfect infinitive; but here ma/xesqai refers to time present relatively to e)/fh; whereas, if it had been used as an
imperfect, it would have referred to time past relatively to e)/fh, as in e)/fh to\
stra/teuma th=| proterai/a| ma/xesqai, he said that the army had been fighting on the day
before. In the former case the direct discourse was ma/xetai, in the latter it was
e)ma/xeto. Such an imperfect infinitive differs from the aorist
in the same construction only by expressing the duration or repetition
of an action (as in the indicative); it gives, in fact, the only means
of representing in the infinitive what is usually expressed by le/gei o(/ti e)poi/ei, he says that he was doing, as opposed to
le/gei o(/ti e)poi/hsen,
he says that he did. (For the similar
use of the present optative to represent the imperfect, see 116, 4.) This
construction is never used unless the context makes it certain that the
infinitive represents an imperfect and not a present, so that no
ambiguity can arise. See the examples.

So sometimes in Latin:

Q. Scaevolam memoria teneo bello
Marsico, cum esset summa senectute, cotidie facere omnibus conveniendi potestatem sui.

CIC. Phil.
viii. 31.
So

Q. Maximum accepimus facile celare, tacere, dissimulare, insidiari,
praeripere hostium consilia.

CIC. de Off.
i. 108.

§125

The context must decide whether an aorist optative in an
indirect question represents the aorist subjunctive (as in 3) or the
aorist indicative (as in the last examples under 1). Thus the first
example under 3 might mean they asked whether
they had given up their city, pare/domen th\n po/lin; But in most cases
the aorist subjunctive is the direct form implied, and an aorist
indicative used in a direct question is generally retained; ei) a)napleu/seien in 1 is,
therefore, exceptional.

§127

Although the usage of the language is very strict, by which
the aorist infinitive after verbs of saying,
thinking, etc. is past, as representing an aorist
indicative, still several passages are found, even in the best authors,
in which an aorist infinitive after such verbs as nomi/zw, oi)/omai, and even fhmi/ refers to future time.
Many critics, especially Madvig, [note: See Madvig's Bemerkungen über einige Puncte der griechischen
Wortfügungslehre, pp. 34-44: Griech. Syntax, § 172a Anm.]
deny the existence of this anomaly, and emend the offending aorists to
the future or insert a)/n.
If they are allowed (and most of the passages still stand uncorrected in
many editions), they must be treated as strictly exceptional; and no
principle, and no consistent exception to the general principle, can be
based on them. E.g.

*fa/to ga\r ti/sasqai
a)lei/tas,

for he said that he should punish the
offenders.

xx. 121.
(In

ti/sasqai in

me/myasqai *)apri/hn [note: (sc. a)pekri/nato）] : pare/sesqai ga\r kai\
au)to\s kai\ a)/llous a)/cein,

not have reason to blame him; for he not only would be

## Future Optative.

§128

The future optative is used chiefly in indirect discourse
after past tenses, to represent a future indicative of the direct form.
Even here the future indicative is generally retained (670, b). E.g.

*(upeipw\n ta)/lla o(/ti
au)to\s ta)kei= pra/coi, w)/|xeto,

have pra/cei in the
indirect form. See, in the same chapter, a)pokrina/menoi o(/ti pe/myousin,
having replied that they would
send, where pe/myoien might have been used.)

*ei)/ tina feu/gonta
lh/yoito, prohgo/reuen o(/ti w(s polemi/w| xrh/soito

o)/yointo

§129

The future optative occurs first in Pindar, in an indirect
question,

e)ke/leusen diakri=nai a(/ntina
sxh/soi tis h(rw/wn,

should take
[note: （ti/na sxh/sei;),]

Py. ix.
126
. It is used chiefly by the Attic prose writers, as the
correlative of the future indicative, that tense having had no
corresponding optative form in the older language, as the present,
perfect, and aorist indicative and subjunctive had. It is never used
with a)/n.

future optative is found in object clauses with o(/pws after verbs of striving, etc. (339). Here its use is closely akin to that in

## Future Infinitive.

§135

The future infinitive is regularly used only in indirect
discourse (111,
112), where it
always represents a future indicative of the direct form. E.g. *gra/yein fhsi/n, he says that he will write;
gra/yein e)/fh, he said that he would write;
gra/yein fh/sei, he will say that he will write: all
representing gra/yw, I will write.

*pollou/s ge e)/sesqai e)/legon
tou\s e)qelh/sontas,

they said that there would be many who would
be willing.

iii. 2, 26.

§136

Verbs of hoping, expecting, promising,
swearing, and a few others of like meaning, form an

infinitive in indirect discourse; but they also allow the aorist and

[section 31]

## Future Perfect.

§137

The future perfect of the dependent moods is rare, except in
verbs whose perfect has the meaning of a present (49), where it is an ordinary
future (82).

When it occurs in other verbs, it is only in the infinitive
of indirect discourse. E.g.

*tau=ta （ e)/fh ）
pepra/cesqai duoi=n h)\ triw=n h(merw=n,

he said that we should see these things
already accomplished within two or three days.

DEM. xix.
74.
(Here the direct discourse was pepra/cetai tau=ta, these things will have been already accomplished.）

[section 32]

## III. Tenses of the Participle.

§138

The tenses of the participle generally express time present,
past, or future relatively to the time of the verb with which they are
connected.

The uses of the participle with a)/n are not included here. For these see
Chapter III.

[section 33]

## Present Participle.

§139

The present participle generally represents an action as
going on at the time of its leading verb. E.g.

*tou=to
poiou=sin nomi/zontes di/kaion ei)=nai, they do this thinking it is just.

general.

(*strathgou=ntos is present relatively to e)pra/xqh.)

*kai/toi tau=ta pra/ttwn

*tau=ta periidei=n

xviii. 63.

## Perfect Participle.

*)epainou=si tou\s ei)rhko/tas, they praise those who have spoken.

## Future Participle.

§153

The future participle represents an action as future with
reference to the time of its leading verb. E.g. *tou=to poih/swn e)/rxetai, he is coming to do this;
tou=to poih/swn h)=lqen,
he came to do this.
*pemfqh/setai tau=ta e)rw=n,
he will be sent to say this.
*oi)=da au)to\n tou=to
poih/sonta, I know that he will do this;
oi)=da tou=to poih/swn,
I know that I shall do this;
h)/|dein au)to\n tou=to
poih/sonta, I knew that he would do
this.

For the various uses of the future participle, and examples,
see Chapter VI.

[section 37]

## Gnomic and Iterative tenses: Gnomic Aorist and Perfect.

§154

The aorist and sometimes the perfect indicative are used in
animated language to express general truths.
These are called the gnomic aorist and the
gnomic perfect, and are usually to be
translated by our present.

§155

These tenses give a more vivid statement of general truths,
by employing a distinct case or several distinct cases in the past to
represent (as it were) all possible cases, and implying that what has
occurred is likely to occur again under similar circumstances. E.g.

*ka/tqan' o(mw=s o(/ t' a)ergo\s
a)nh\r o(/ te polla\ e)orgw/s,

the idle man and he who has laboured much
alike must die.

§157

General truths are more commonly expressed in Greek, as in
English, by the present. The present and aorist appear together above,
in nearly the same sense; the gnomic aorist is, however, commonly
distinguished from the present by referring to a single or a sudden
occurrence, while the present (as usual) implies duration. Thus in
DEM. ii. 10,
above, the aorist h)/nqhsen
implies a sudden blossoming out with hopes,
as opposed to the continuance or repetition expressed by a)nte/xei, hold out, fwra=tai, are
detected, and katarrei=, fall in ruin.

§158

An aorist somewhat resembling the gnomic is very common in
Homeric similes, where it is usually to be
translated by the present. E.g. *)/hripe d' w(s o(/te tis dru=s h)/ripen, and he fell, as when an
oak falls, (literally, as when an oak
once fell).
Il. xiii. 389.

This can better be seen in the longer and more complicated
examples which are quoted under 547 and 548.

[section 39]

## Dependence of Moods and Tenses.

§165

In dependent sentences, where the construction allows both
the subjunctive and the optative, the subjunctive is used if the leading
verb is primary, and the optative if it is secondary. (See 21.) E.g. *pra/ttousin a(\ a)\n
bou/lwntai, they do whatever they
please; but e)/pratton a(\
bou/lointo, they did whatever they
pleased.

§166

In like manner, where the construction allows both the
indicative and the optative, the indicative follows primary, and the
optative follows secondary tenses. E.g. *le/gousin o(/ti tou=to bou/lontai, they say that they wish for this;
e)/lecan o(/ti tou=to
bou/lointo, they said that they wished
for this.

§167

To these fundamental rules we find one special exception. In
indirect discourse of all kinds (including sentences denoting a purpose or object
after i(/na, o(/pws, mh/,
etc.) either an indicative or a subjunctive may depend upon a secondary
tense, so that the mood and tense actually used by the speaker may be
retained in the indirect form. (See 667, 1.) E.g. *ei)=pen o(/ti bou/letai, for ei)=pen o(/ti bou/loito, he said that he wished (i.e. he said
bou/lomai). *)efobei=to mh\ tou=to
ge/nhtai, for e)fobei=to mh\
tou=to ge/noito, he feared lest it
should happen (i.e. he thought,
fobou=mai mh\ ge/nhtai).
(See 318.)

§168

An only apparent exception occurs

stands in a dependent sentence. In both these cases the original form is

§169

It is therefore important to ascertain which tenses (in all
the moods) are followed, in dependent sentences, as primary tenses by
the indicative or subjunctive, and which as secondary tenses by the
optative.

[section 40]

## Indicative.

§170

In the indicative the general rule holds, that the present,
perfect, future, and future perfect are primary, and the imperfect,
pluperfect, and aorist are secondary tenses.

§171

But the historical present is a secondary tense, as it refers
to the past; and the gnomic aorist is a primary tense, as it refers to
the present.

[section 42]

## Optative.

§176

As the optative refers sometimes to the future and sometimes
to the past, it exerts upon a dependent verb sometimes the force of a
primary, and sometimes that of a secondary tense.

When A. it refers to the past, as in
general suppositions with ei) and relatives after past tenses, or when it takes its time
from a past verb (as in a final clause), it has the force of a secondary
tense.

When B. it refers to the future, as in
future conditions, in its use with a)/n, and in wishes, it is properly to be considered
primary. In many cases, however, a double construction is here allowed.
On the principle of assimilation the Greeks preferred the optative to
the subjunctive in certain clauses depending on an optative, the
dependent verb referring to the future like the leading verb, and
differing little from a subjunctive in such a position. A dependent
indicative is, however, very seldom assimilated to a leading optative.
Such assimilation of a dependent verb to an optative takes place (1)
regularly in protasis and conditional
relative clauses depending on an optative of future time; (2)
seldom in final and object clauses after
i(/na, o(/pws, mh/,
etc.; (3)
very rarely in the case of the indicative in
indirect quotations or questions, but (4) more freely in the case of the subjunctive
in indirect questions.

These four classes of sentences which depend on an optative
referring to the future are treated separately below (I.-IV.)

§177

conditional relative sentences depending upon an optative which refers to the future, the optative rather than

§191

The tenses of the infinitive and participle with a)/n are followed, in dependent

they represent, if these stood in the same position. See Chapter III.

[chapter 3]

## Chapter III

[section 44]

## The Particle a)/n.

§192

The adverb a)/n
(with the epic ke/, Doric
ka/) has two uses, which
must be distinguished.

1. In one use, it denotes that the action of the verb to
which it is joined is dependent upon some condition, expressed or
implied. This is its force with the secondary tenses of the indicative,
and with the optative, infinitive, and participle: with these it belongs
strictly to the verb, to which it gives a potential force, like our
would.

2. In its other use, it is joined regularly to ei), if, to relative and temporal words, and sometimes to the final
particles w(s, o(/pws, and
o)/fra, when any of
these are followed by the subjunctive. Here, although as an adverb it
qualifies the verb, it is so closely connected with the relative or
particle, that it often coalesces with it, forming e)a/n, h)/n, a_)/n o(/tan, o(po/tan, e)peida/n,
e)pa/n or e)ph/n
(Ionic e)pea/n).

These statements include only the constructions which are in
good use in Attic Greek. For the epic use of ke/ or a)/n with the subjunctive in a potential sense (as with the
optative) see 201,
1; for ke/ or a)/n with the future indicative
see 196.

§193

There is no word or expression in English which can be used
separately to translate a)/n. In its first use (192, 1) we express it by the form of
the verb which we use; as e)/lqoi
a)/n, he would go; h)=lqen a)/n, he would have gone. In its second use, with
the subjunctive, it generally has no force that can be made perceptible
in translation.

The peculiar use of a)/n can be understood only by a study of the various
constructions in which it occurs. These are enumerated below, with
references (when it is necessary) to the more full explanation of each
in Chapter IV.

§194

No theory of the origin of either a)/n or ke/ has yet helped to explain their meaning, however
valuable the discussion of the question may have been to comparative
philology. It seems to be clear that ke/ is the older particle; it occurs 621 times in Homer
while a)/n occurs 155 times;
in Pindar the two are nearly balanced; a)/n has a preference for negative
sentences, being very often attached to the negative; a)/n is more emphatic, as
appears indeed from its fixed accent, while ke/ is enclitic; ke/ is much more frequent than a)/n in relative clauses in
Homer. [note: See Monro, Homeric Grammar, pp.
265-267. For Pindar, see Gildersleeve in Jour. Phil. iii. pp. 446-455, where may be found a
complete enumeration of the passages in Pindar containing either
a)/n (30 cases) or
ke/ (33
cases).] But, practically, it is still safe to assume that the two
particles are used in substantially the same sense in all epic and lyric
poetry. In Herodotus and Attic Greek only a)/n is used.

[section 45]

## Indicative with a)/n.

§195

The present and perfect indicative are never used with a)/n.

This seems to occur chiefly when Plato and Aristotle use
ka)\n ei) (= kai\ a)\n, ei)) like kai\ ei), without regard to the
mood of the verb which is to follow, to which ka)/n really belongs. See

PLAT. Men. 72
C,

ka)\n ei) pollai/ ei)sin, e(/n
ge/ ti ei)=dos tau)to\n pa=sai e)/xousi
, i.e. even if they are many, still (it
would seem to follow that) they all have one and the same
form. So
PLAT. Rep. 579 D,
Soph. 247E. So

ARISTOT.

ka)\n ei) plei/ous
, with skepte/on
e)sti/n.

Examples of a different class (without ka)\n ei)) are obviously corrupt, and have
now almost disappeared from our texts. One of the last relics,

Leg. 712E,

a)\n e)rwthqei\s o)/ntws o(/per ei)=pon, ou)k e)/xw
ei)pei=n
, is now simply emended by reading a)nerwthqei/s.

[section 46]

## Subjunctive and Optative with a)/n.

§200

In Attic Greek a)/n is regularly used with the subjunctive in protasis and in
conditional relative sentences, and sometimes in final clauses with
w(s and o(/pws, being always closely
joined with the particle or the relative; but never in independent
sentences. See 325,
381, and 522.

§201

1. In epic poetry, when the independent subjunctive has
nearly the sense of the future indicative (284), it sometimes takes ke/ or a)/n. This forms a future potential
expression, nearly equivalent to the future indicative with ke/ or a)/n, and sometimes approaching the optative
with ke/ or a)/n. E.g.

*ei) de/ ke mh\ dw/h|sin, e)gw\
de/ ken au)to\s e(/lwmai,

and if he does not give her up, I will take
her myself.

Il. i.
324
; see also
i. 137.

See 285
and 452. For the
variety of nearly equivalent future potential forms which the Homeric
language presents, reduced to one in Attic Greek, see 235.

2. The epic language has ke/ or a)/n
with the subjunctive in the constructions of 192, 2; but its use of ke/ or a)/n in conditions is less strict, and that
with final particles is more free, than the Attic use of a)/n.

See 325-328; 450-454; 468-471; 538-541.

§202

The optative with a)/n forms the apodosis of the less vivid future condition
(like the English form with would or should), or has a potential sense. E.g. *ei) tou=to poih/seien, a)/qlios a)\n
ei)/h, if he should do this,
he would be wretched.
*(hde/ws a)\n e)roi/mhn
au)to/n, I should like to ask
him. (See
233 and 455.)

For construction of a)/n or ke/ with
ei) or the final
particles and the optative, see 460; and 329, 330, 349, 350, 351.

§203

As the future optative came into common use after the future
indicative with a)/n
(196) was nearly
extinct, it was never used with a)/n.

[section 47]

## Infinitive with a)/n.

§204

The infinitive can be used with a)/n in all cases in which a finite verb
would have a)/n if it stood
in its place.

This is found chiefly in indirect discourse, in which each
tense of the infinitive with a)/n represents the corresponding
tenses of the indicative or optative with a)/n in the direct form. The context must
decide whether the indicative or optative is represented in each
case.

## Participle with a)/n.

§213

When the participle is used with a)/n, each tense represents the
corresponding tenses of the indicative or optative with a)/n.

The participle with a)/n is not, like the infinitive with a)/n, found chiefly in indirect discourse;
but a)/n is more frequently
added to an attributive or a circumstantial participle (822) to give it a potential force
equivalent to that of the indicative or optative with a)/n. The participle with
a)/n is not found in
Homer or Pindar.

[chapter 4]

## Chapter IV

[section 52]

## Use of the Moods.

§230

This chapter treats of all constructions which require any
other form of the finite verb than the simple indicative in absolute
assertions and direct questions (2). The infinitive and participle are included
here so far as either of them is used in indirect discourse, in protasis
or apodosis, and in other constructions (as with pri/n and w(/ste) in which the finite moods also are
used.

§231

These constructions are discussed under the following
heads:—

I. The potential optative and indicative.

II. The imperative and subjunctive in commands, exhortations,
and prohibitions.—Subjunctive and indicative with mh/ and mh\ ou) in cautious assertions.—
*(/opws and o(/pws mh/ with the independent
future indicative or subjunctive.

III. The subjunctive (like the future indicative) in
independent sentences.—The interrogative subjunctive.

IV. *ou) mh/ with
the subjunctive or future indicative.

V. Final and object clauses after i(/na, w(s, o(/pws, o)/fra, and mh/.

VI. Conditional sentences.

VII. Relative and temporal sentences, including consecutive
sentences with w(/ste, etc.

VIII. Indirect discourse.

IX. Causal sentences.

X. Expressions of a wish.

[section 53]

## Section I: The Potential Optative and Indicative.

§232

We find fully established in the Homeric language a use of
the optative and the past tenses of the indicative with a)/n or ke/, which expresses the action of the verb
as dependent on circumstances or conditions; as e)/lqoi a)/n, he
might (could or would) go;
h)=lqen a)/n, he might (could
or would) have
gone. Such an optative or indicative is called potential.

[section 54]

## I. Potential Optative.

§233

It has already been seen (13) that Homer sometimes uses the optative in a
weak future sense, without ke/ or a)/n, to
express a concession or permission. Such neutral forms seem to form a
connecting link between the simple optative in wishes and the optative
with a)/n, partaking to a
certain extent of the nature of both. (For a full discussion of these
forms and their relations, see Appendix I.) Such expressions seem to
show that the early language used forms like e)/lqoimi and i)/doimi in two senses, I may go and I may see, or may I go and may I
see, corresponding to e)/lqw and i)/dw in
their two Homeric senses I shall go and
I shall see
(284), or let me go and let me see
(257).

§234

The neutral optatives like
Il. iv. 18 are rare even in
Homer, the language having already distinguished the two meanings in
sense, and marked them in most cases by external signs. The optative
expressing what may happen in the future took the particle ke/ or a)/n, and was negatived by ou), denoting the relations
which we express by our potential mood with may,
can, might, could, would, and should. Thus e(/loimi/ ke
h)/ ken a(loi/hn, I may slay or I may
be slain,
Il. xxii. 253; a)nh\r de/ ken ou)/ ti *dio\s no/on
ei)ru/ssaito, a man cannot contend
against the will of Zeus,
Il. viii. 143. [note: When the idea of
ability, possibility, or necessity is the chief element in the
expression, and is not (as above) merely auxiliary, it is expressed
by a special verb like du/namai,
dei=, or xrh/. Especially, the idea of obligation is generally expressed by dei= or xrh/ with the infinitive; as

tou=de xrh\ klu/ein,

him we must obey,

SOPH. Ant.
666.
] On the other hand, the simple optative (without
ke/ or a)/n) was more and more
restricted to the expression of a wish or exhortation, and was negatived
by mh/; as mh\ ge/noito, may it not happen,

pi/qoio/ moi,

listen to me

(Hom. Od. iv.
193)
, as opposed to ou)k a)\n
ge/noito, it could not
happen. The potential forms e)/lqoimi a)/n and i)/doimi a)/n differ from the more absolute future
indicative and the old subjunctive forms e)/lqw and i)/dw, I shall
go and I shall see, by expressing a
future act as dependent on some future circumstances or conditions,
which may be more or less distinctly implied. The freedom of the earlier
language extended the use of the potential optative to present and
sometimes even to past time. See 438 and 440.

§235

In most cases the limiting condition involved in the
potential optative is not present to the mind in any definite form, and
can be expressed in English only by such words as perchance, possibly, or probably, or by the auxiliaries could,
would, should, might, etc. with the vague conditions which
these imply (like if he should try, if he pleased,
if he could, if what is natural should happen, etc.)
Sometimes a more general condition is implied, like in any possible case; as ou)k a)\n dexoi/mhn tou=to, I would
not accept this (on any terms);
here the expression becomes nearly absolute, and may often be translated
by our future, as ou)k a)\n
meqei/mhn tou= qro/nou, I will not
give up the throne (
AR. Ran. 830), or (in positive
sentences) by must, as pa/ntes qauma/zoien a)\n tou=to, all must admire this.

The optative thus used with no conscious feeling of any definite condition, but still implying that
the statement is conditioned and not absolute, is the simplest and most
primitive potential optative. It is equivalent to the Latin potential
subjunctive, as credas,
dicas, cernas, putes, etc., you
may believe, say, perceive, think, etc. The Homeric language
has six forms, all expressing futurity with different degrees of
absoluteness and distinctness; as o)/yomai, o)/yomai/ ke, i)/dwmai, i)/dwmai/ ke, i)doi/mhn,
i)doi/mhn ke (or a)/n), containing every step from I shall
see to I should see. Of these
only the first and the last (with a tradition of the second) survived
the Homeric period, and the others (especially the fifth) were already
disappearing during that period (240), being found unnecessary as the language
became settled, and as the optative with ke/ or a)/n became more fixed as a future potential form.

§236

In the following examples of the potential optative no
definite form of condition is present to the mind:—

*)emoi\ de\ to/t' a)\n polu\
ke/rdion ei)/h,

profit me far more.

Il. xxii.
108.

*feu/gwmen: e)/ti ga/r ken
a)lu/caimen kako\n h)=mar,

let us flee; for perchance we may still
escape the evil day.

Od. x.
269.

*plhsi/on a)llh/lwn: kai/ ken
dioi+steu/seias,

the rocks are close together: you might
perhaps shoot an arrow across the space.

Od. xii.
102.
So
Od.
xxiii. 125.

*ou)kou=n po/rois a)\n th/nde
dwrea\n e)moi/;

AESCH. Prom.
616.

pa=n ga\r a)\n .pu/qoio/ mou,

*ti/ to/nd' a)\n ei)/pois

§239

The potential optative may express every grade of
potentiality from the almost pure future ou)k a)\n meqei/mhn, I will not give up (under any
circumstances), to

ou)k a)\n dikai/ws e)s kako\n
pe/soimi/ ti,

I could not justly fall into any trouble,

SOPH. Ant.
240
, where dikai/ws
points to the substance of a limiting condition, if
justice should be done. From this the step is but slight to
such cases as ou)/te e)sqi/ousi
plei/w h)\ du/nantai fe/rein: diarragei=en ga\r a)/n, they do not eat more than they can carry;
for (if they should) they would burst,
XEN. Cyr. viii. 2, 21 , where
ei) . . . e)sqi/oien is
necessary to complete the sense and is clearly understood from the
preceding words. A final step in the same direction is taken when the
condition is actually stated as part of the sentence. As e)/lqoi a)/n means he would go (under some future circumstances),
if these limiting circumstances are to be definitely expressed it is
natural to use the corresponding form of condition, ei) with the optative, as ei) keleu/seias e)/lqoi a)/n,
if you should command he would go.
The protasis is thus assimilated to the apodosis in form, as it conforms
to it in sense and general character. So when a conclusion is to follow
such a condition as ei)
keleu/seias, the corresponding optative with a)/n, i.e.
the potential optative, is naturally chosen, although nothing but regard
to harmony and symmetry makes either if you should
command he will go or if you command he
would go, or the equivalent Greek forms, objectionable. In
fact, these very forms are far more common in the more fluid Homeric
language than in the fixed and regular style of Attic prose. There is,
therefore, no necessary or logical bond of union between two forms like
ei) keleu/seias and
e)/lqoi a)/n. This
connexion is, indeed, far more the effect of assimilation in form, as
appears especially when the apodosis contains an optative in a wish; as
in

w(s a)po/loito kai\ a)/llos
o(/tis toiau=ta/ ge r(e/zoi,

may another perish also who shall do the like

(Hom. Od. i.
47)
, where if a)pole/sqw
had been used we should naturally have had r(e/zh|.

For examples of the optative with a)/n or ke/ with a definite protasis expressed or implied in the
context, see 455
and 472.

## II. Potential Indicative.

§243

As the potential optative represents a future act as
dependent on future circumstances (234), so the potential indicative originally
represents a past act as dependent on past circumstances. Therefore,
while h)=lqen means he went, h)=lqen a)/n means he would have
gone (under some past circumstances).
It is probable that no definite limiting circumstances were present to
the mind when this form first came into use, so that h)=lqen a)/n naturally signified merely that
it was likely, possible, or probable that he went or (as we express it)
that he might have gone or would have been likely to go, sometimes that
he must have gone.

In this sense it appears as a past form of the potential
optative, e.g. of e)/lqoi
a)/n in the sense he might perchance
go or he would be likely to go (in
the future). The same relation appears in Latin, where credas, putes, cernas, dicas, you would be
likely to believe, think, etc., are transferred to past time
as crederes, putares, cerneres,
diceres, you would have believed,
thought, etc. [note: We are probably justified in assuming that the past
meaning which here appears in crederes, etc. is the original meaning of the Latin
imperfect subjunctive in this use, as it certainly is that of the
Greek imperfect indicative with a)/n. See 435.] Here putet and putaret are precisely equivalent to oi)/oito a)/n, he
would be likely to think, and w)/|eto a)/n, he
would have been likely to think.

§244

We find the potential indicative in its simplest use (last
mentioned)—with no reference to any definite condition, but
merely expressing past possibility, probability, or necessity— in
all classes of Greek writers. E.g. *ou)d' a)\n e)/ti fra/dmwn per a)nh\r *sarphdo/na di=on e)/gnw,

Sarpedon.

§245

In most cases of the past tenses of the indicative with
a)/n there is at least
an implied reference to some supposed circumstances different from the
real ones, so that h)=lqen
a)/n commonly means he would have
gone (if something had not been as it
was). When we speak of a past event as subject to conditions, we
are apt to imply that the conditions were not fulfilled, as otherwise
they would not be alluded to. This reference to an unfulfilled
condition, however, does not make it necessary that the action of the
potential indicative itself should be unreal, although this is generally
the case. (See
412.) The unfulfilled past condition to which the potential
indicative refers may be as vague and indistinct as the future condition
to which the potential optative refers (235); as if he had wished,
if he had tried, if it had been possible, in any case, and
others which are implied in our auxiliaries might,
could, would, should, etc., but are seldom expressed by us in
words. Compare ou)de\n a)\n kako\n
poih/seian, they could do no
harm (i.e. if they should try), with
ou)de\n a)\n kako\n
e)poi/hsan, they could have done no
harm (i.e. if they had tried). E.g.

*ou) ga/r ken duna/mesqa qura/wn
u(yhla/wn a)pw/sasqai li/qon,

for we could not have moved the stone from
the high doorway.

Od. ix.
304.

§248

The final step is taken when an unreal condition is expressed
as part of the sentence, forming the protasis to which the potential
indicative is the apodosis; as h)=lqen a)\n ei) e)ke/leusa, he
would have gone if I had commanded him. The dependent
protasis, by a natural assimilation, has a past tense of the indicative
corresponding to the form of the apodosis. On the other hand, when an
unreal condition has been expressed, as ei) e)ke/leusa, the potential indicative is
the natural form to state what would have
been the result if the condition had been fulfilled. (See 390, 2; and
410.) The potential indicative does not change its essential nature by
being thus made part of an unreal conditional expression, and it is not
necessarily implied that its action did not take place (see 412).
Although the latter is generally implied or inferred, while the reverse
seldom occurs, still it is important to a true understanding of the
nature of the indicative with a)/n to remember that it is not essential or necessary for it
either to refer to an unreal condition or to denote in itself what is
contrary to fact.

For a periphrastic form of potential indicative with e)/dei, xrh=n, etc., with the
infinitive, see
415.

For the Homeric use of the present optative with ke/ or a)/n as a present potential form (like the
later imperfect with a)/n),
see 438.

For the rare Homeric optative with ke/ in the sense of the past tenses of the
indicative with ke/ or
a)/n, see 440.

§249

From the primitive use of the past tenses of the indicative
to express what was likely to occur under past
circumstances, we may explain the iterative use of these
tenses with a)/n
(162), which is
generally thought to have no connection with the potential indicative
with a)/n. Thus h)=lqen a)/n, meaning
originally he would have gone (under some past circumstances), might easily
come to have a frequentative sense, he would have
gone (under all circumstances or
whenever occasion offered), and hence to
mean he used to go. See
SOPH. Ph.
443, o(\s ou)k a)\n ei(/let'
ei)sa/pac ei)pei=n, o(/pou mhdei\s e)w/|h, (Thersites) who used never to be content to speak but once when
all forbade him (lit. when nobody
permitted him). Originally ou)k a)\n ei(/leto would mean he would not have been content (under any circumstances), hence he was never content. The optative e)w/|h
(532) shows the
nature of the expression here. See the examples under 162, and the last
example under 244.

This construction is not Homeric; but it is found in
Herodotus and is common in Attic Greek. There is no difficulty in
understanding it as an offshoot of the potential indicative, when it is
seen that the latter did not involve originally any denial of its own
action.

In these examples sometimes the fear itself, and sometimes

§262

(a) By prefixing dei/dw or fobou=mai
to any of the subjunctives with mh/ in 261, we get the full construction with verbs of fearing;
as dei/dw mh\ nh=as e(/lwsi,
I fear they may seize the ships, in
which mh\ e(/lwsi represents
an original construction which at first followed dei/dw paratactically—I fear: may they not seize the ships—
and afterwards became welded with it as a dependent clause. So if
dei/dw were removed from
a sentence like dei/dw mh/ ti
pa/qh|sin,
Il. xi. 470, we should have an independent
clause like those quoted above. See mh\ dama/ssh| and dei/dw mh\ ge/nwmai,
Od. v. 467 and
473.

(b) In like manner, by prefixing other verbs than those of
fearing to such clauses, the original negative final clause with mh/ is developed; as maxou/meqa mh\ nh=as e(/lwsi,
we will fight that they
may not seize the ships. Again, if the
leading clause were removed from a sentence like au)tou= mi/mn' e)pi\ pu/rgw|, mh\ pai=d' o)rfaniko\n
qh/h|s xh/rhn te gunai=ka, remain
here on the tower, lest you make your
child an orphan and your wife a widow,
Il. vi. 431,
there would remain mh/ . . .
qh/h|s, do not make, or may you not make, in the originally
independent form, like the clauses with mh/ in 261. (See 307.)

§263

（*mh\ ou), with the Subjunctive.) The clause with
mh/ expressing desire to
avert an object of fear, in its original simple form as well as in the
developed final construction, may refer to a negative object, and
express fear that something may not happen.
Here mh\ ou) is used with
the subjunctive, like ne
non in Latin.

Thus mh\ nh=as
e(/lwsi being may they not seize the
ships, mh\ ou) nh=as
e(/lwsi would be may they not fail to seize
the ships, implying fear that they may
not seize them. Homer has one case of mh\ ou) after a verb of fearing: dei/dw mh\ ou)/ ti/s toi u(po/sxhtai
to/de e)/rgon,
Il. x. 39.He has several cases of mh\ ou) in final clauses and
one in an object clause (354).
Il. i. 28, mh/ nu/ toi
ou) xrai/smh| skh=ptron kai\ ste/mma qeoi=o, is often cited
as a case of independent mh\
ou), meaning beware lest the staff and
fillet of the God shall prove of no avail to you. So
Delbrück (I. p. 119), who nevertheless quotes
Il. i. 565,
a)ll' a)ke/ousa ka/qhso e)mw=|
d' e)pipei/qeo mu/qw|, mh/ nu/ toi ou) xrai/smwsin o(/soi qeoi/
ei)s' e)n *)olu/mpw|, as containing a dependent final
clause. In the two other cases of mh\ ou) with the subjunctive in Homer,
Il. xv. 164
(an object clause, see 354), and xxiv. 569 (final), the dependence of
the clause with mh\ ou) is
even more obvious; and in
Il. xxiv. 584 we have in mh\ ou)k e)ru/saito the decisive proof that
this clause is felt to be dependent in the change from the subjunctive
to the optative after a past tense. It is therefore more than doubtful
whether mh\ ou) xrai/smh| in

Il. i.
28 is not dependent on mh/ se
kixei/w in vs. 26. Plato in paraphrasing this passage (
Rep. 393E）
takes the clause as final and dependent (see 132). But, whether we have
a case of independent mh\
ou) with the subjunctive in Homer or not, there can be no doubt
that this is the original form from which came the dependent final
clause with mh\ ou).

§264

After Homer we have the independent clause with mh/ in Aeschylus,
Ag. 134 and

## Subjunctive with mh/ and mh\
ou) in Cautious Assertions.

§265

In Herodotus v. 79 we have a)lla\ ma=llon mh\ ou) tou=to h)=| to\
manth/ion, but I suspect rather that this
may prove not to be the meaning of the oracle. This is the
first example of a construction, very common in Plato, used also by
Aristotle, and found once in Demosthenes, in which mh/ with the subjunctive expresses a
suspicion that something may be (or may prove to be) true, and mh\ ou) with the subjunctive a suspicion
that something may not be true; the former
amounting to a cautious assertion, the latter to a cautious negation.
Examples from Plato are:—

§266

In these cautious assertions and negations, although no
desire of the speaker to avert an object of fear is implied, there is
always a tacit allusion to such a desire on the part of some person who
is addressed or referred to, or else an ironical pretence of such a
desire of the speaker himself.

§267

The subjunctive with mh/ in this sense is sometimes found in dependent clauses. E.g.
*(/ora mh\ a)/llo ti to\
gennai=on kai\ to\ a)gaqo\n h)=| tou= sw/|zein kai\
sw/|zesqai, see to it lest (it prove true that) these
may be different things, etc.
PLAT. Gorg. 512D. The common
translation, see whether they may
not be different, gives the general sense,
but not the construction, which is simply that of mh\ a)/llo ti h)=|
(265) transferred
to a dependent clause.

§268

In a few cases Plato has mh/ with the subjunctive in a cautious question with a
negative answer implied. As mh\
a)/llo ti h)=| tou=to means this may
possibly be something else, so the question mh\ a)/llo ti h)=| tou=to;
means can this possibly be something else?
The four examples given by Weber are:—

*mh/ ti a)/llo h)=| para\
tau=ta;

can there be any other besides these?

*)=ara mh\ a)/llo ti h)=| qa/natos
