§445

It will be seen that the apodosis here (444) may consist of any future
expression,—the future indicative, the imperative, the
subjunctive in exhortations and prohibitions, the infinitive in any
future sense, the potential optative with a)/n, or the optative in a wish. It may also
contain a present indicative including a reference to the future, like
xrh/ or dei= or the verbal in te/os, or the present used
emphatically for the future, like o(mologw= above quoted (444) from
XEN. Cyr. v. 5, 13 , or pau=la/ e)sti in
PLAT. Rep.
473D.

§446

The English, especially the colloquial language, seldom
expresses the distinction between this form of the future condition and
the present condition (402). Thus modern custom allows us to use the inexact
expression if he wishes, not merely for
ei) bou/letai, if he now wishes, but also for e)a\n bou/lhtai, if he shall wish. The sense, however,
generally makes the distinction in time clear.

It is worth noting that the Authorised Version of the English
New Testament never uses forms like if he does, if
he is, in either future or present conditions, even when the
Greek has the present indicative with ei); but it has either the subjunctive or
the future indicative in future conditions, and the subjunctive in
present conditions. The Revised Version, on the other hand, admits the
present indicative (as if he is) in present
conditions, but not consistently. See
LUC. xxiii. 35, ei) ou(=to/s e)stin o( *xristo/s, V. A. if he be Christ, R. V. if this is the Christ; but in MATTH. vi. 23, ei) ou)=n to\ fw=s to\ e)n soi\ sko/tos
e)sti/n, both versions have if
therefore the light that is in thee be darkness. See also

Cor. ii.
v. 17.

§447

（Future Indicative in Protasis.）
The future indicative with ei) is often used in the protasis to express a future
condition. This is a still stronger form of expression than the
subjunctive, though it sometimes alternates with it in the same
sentence. Both, however, correspond to the English if I shall do this, if I do this, etc. The future, as an
emphatic form, is especially common when the condition contains a strong
appeal to the feelings or a threat or warning. [note: In

minatory and monitory conditions: see Gildersleeve in Trans. of Assoc. Phil. for 1876, p. 13.
This article contains an enumeration of all the cases of e)a/n with the subjunctive
in future conditions and of ei) with the future indicative in the three tragedians. It
appears that in Aeschylus there are 22 cases of the future and only
8 of the subjunctive; in Sophocles 67 futures and 55 subjunctives;
in Euripides 131 futures and 177 subjunctives. If we omit the
futures which are equivalent to me/llw with an infinitive, for which the subjunctive
could not be substituted (see 407), we have in Aeschylus 15 futures
in future conditions and 8 subjunctives; in Sophocles 46 and 55; in
Euripides 98 and 177. In Attic prose Thucydides and Lysias have the
largest proportion of futures; but in prose, as in Aristophanes, the
subjunctives always preponderate.] It is thus a favourite
construction with the tragedians. E.g. *ei) ga\r *)axilleu\s oi)=os e)pi\ *trw/essi
maxei=tai, ou)de\ mi/nunq' e(/cousi podw/kea *phlei+/wna,

§456

This form of the conditional sentence in its fully developed
use, as it appears in Attic Greek, must be carefully distinguished from
that of 410; the more so, as we often translate both ei)/h a)/n and h)=n a)/n by the same English expression,
it would be; although the latter implies
that the supposition of the protasis is a false one, while the former
implies no opinion of the speaker as to the truth of the supposition. We
have seen (438-440) that the more primitive Homeric language had not yet
fully separated these two constructions, and still used the optative in
the apodosis of present, and sometimes of past, unreal conditions.

On the other hand, the distinction between this form and that
of 444 is less marked, and it is sometimes of slight importance which of
the two is used. As it is often nearly indifferent in English whether we
say if we shall go (or if we go) it will be well, or
if we should go it would be well, so may
it be in Greek whether we say e)a\n
e)/lqwmen
kalw=s e(/cei or ei) e)/lqoimen kalw=s a)\n
e)/xoi. In writing Greek, this distinction can generally be made
by first observing the form of the apodosis in English; if that is
expressed by should or would, it is to be translated by the Greek optative with
a)/n; if it is expressed
by shall or will, by the future indicative. Other forms of the apodosis, as
the imperative, will present no difficulty. The form to be used in the
protasis will then appear from the principles of the dependence of moods
(170-178); the optative will require another optative with ei) in the dependent protasis,
while the future indicative or any other primary form will require a
subjunctive with e)a/n or a
future indicative with ei).

§457

In indirect discourse after past tenses we often find an
optative in protasis, which merely represents the same tense of the
subjunctive or indicative in the direct discourse. See 667, 1; 689; 694.

For the occasional omission of a)/n in an apodosis of this kind, see 240-242.

§458

The potential optative with a)/n may stand in the protasis with ei); as in ei) e)/lqoimi a)/n, supposing that I would go, easily distinguished from ei) e)/lqoimi, supposing that I should go. Such an
expression does not belong here, but is really a present condition. (See
409; 506.)

§459

The future optative cannot be used in protasis or apodosis,
except in indirect discourse to represent a future indicative of the
direct discourse. (See
128 and 203.)

## II. Present and Past General Suppositions.

§462

In present or past general suppositions, the apodosis
expresses a customary or repeated action or a general truth in present or past time, and the protasis
refers in a general way to any act or acts
of a given class. Here the protasis has the subjunctive with e)a/n after present tenses, and
the optative with ei) after
past tenses. The apodosis has the present or imperfect indicative, or
some other form which implies repetition. E.g. *)\hn e)ggu\s e)/lqh| qa/natos, ou)dei\s bou/letai

no one is (ever) willing to die.

§472

[section 100]

## Substitution and Ellipsis in Apodosis.

§479

The apodosis, in any of its forms, may be expressed by an
infinitive or participle, if the structure of the sentence requires it.

1. It may be expressed by the infinitive or participle in
indirect discourse, each tense representing its own tenses of the
indicative or optative, the present including the imperfect, and the
perfect the pluperfect. If the finite verb in the apodosis would have
taken a)/n, this particle is
used with the infinitive or participle. E.g. *(hgou=mai, ei) tou=to poiei=te, pa/nta kalw=s
e)/xein, I believe that, if you are
doing this, all is well.
*(hgou=mai, e)a\n tou=to poih=te,
pa/nta kalw=s e(/cein, I believe
that, if you (shall) do this, all will be well.
*(hgou=mai, ei) tou=to poioi=te,
pa/nta kalw=s a)\n e)/xein, I believe
that, if you should do this, all would be well.
*(hgou=mai, ei) tou=to e)poih/sate,
pa/nta kalw=s a)\n e)/xein, I believe
that, if you had done this, all would now be (or would have been)
well.
*oi)=da u(ma=s, e)a\n tou=to
poih=te, eu)= pra/contas, I know
that, if you do this, you will prosper.

*pw=s ga\r oi)/esqe
dusxerw=s a)kou/ein *)olunqi/ous, ei)/ ti/s ti le/goi kata\
*fili/ppou kat' e)kei/nous tou\s xro/nous;

how unwillingly do you think the O. heard it, if
any one said anything against Philip in those times?

DEM. vi. 20.
(Here a)kou/ein represents
the imperfect h)/kouon, and
ei) le/goi is a general
supposition, 462.）

For examples of each tense of the infinitive and participle,
see 689. For
the use of each tense of the infinitive or participle with a)/n and examples, see 204-208; 213-216.

2. It may be expressed by the infinitive in any of its
various constructions out of indirect discourse, especially by one
depending on a verb of wishing, commanding,
advising, preparing, etc., from which the infinitive receives
a future meaning. Such an infinitive is a common form of future apodosis
with a protasis in the subjunctive or indicative. E.g. *bou/letai e)lqei=n e)a\n tou=to
ge/nhtai, he wishes to go if this
shall be done.
*paraskeuazo/meqa a)pelqei=n h)\n
dunw/meqa, we are preparing to depart
if we shall be able.
*keleu/ei se a)pelqei=n ei)
bou/lei, he bids you depart if you
please. (See
403 and 445.）

3. The apodosis may be expressed in an attributive or
circumstantial participle. E.g. *(ra|di/ws a)\n a)feqei\s ei) kai\ metri/ws ti tou/twn e)poi/hse,
proei/leto a)poqanei=n, whereas he
might easily have been acquitted [note: （a)fei/qh a)/n）] , if he had
done any of these things even in a moderate degree, he chose to die.

[section 101]

## Apodosis contained in the Protasis.

§486

A protasis may depend on a verb which is not its apodosis,
the real apodosis being so distinctly implied in the form of expression
that it need not be stated separately.

§487

1. This is found especially in Homer, where ei)/ ke (ai)/ ke) or h)/n (without an expressed apodosis) often
seems to have the force of in the hope that;
as in patro\s e)mou= kle/os
mete/rxomai, h)/n pou a)kou/sw, I am
going to seek tidings of my father, if
I shall chance to hear of him, i.e. that
I may hear of him if perchance I shall, or in the hope that I shall hear of him (
Od. iii. 83).
Here the protasis carries with it its own apodosis, which consists of an
implied idea of purpose. [note: The English
translation of certain conditional clauses in the New Testament
which have this peculiar construction preserves the sense of purpose
or desire with the original form of protasis. Thus, that they should seek the Lord, if haply they
might feel after him and find him, Acts xvii. 27; and
he came (to the fig tree), if haply he might find anything thereon,
MARK xi. 13.] The whole sentence (both protasis and apodosis)
is thus condensed into the protasis; but the apodosis is always felt in
the implied idea of purpose or desire which is inherent in the idiom. As
we have seen (312,
Od.
2) that final clauses with a)/n or ke/ and the subjunctive originally included both a
conditional relative clause and a final sentence, so here we have both a
conditional and a final force included under a single conditional form;
and this double force is felt also in the English translation, if haply, in the hope that, in case that, etc.
E.g. *au)ta\r soi\ pukinw=s
u(poqh/someq), ai)/ ke pi/qhai, but
we will make you a wise suggestion, for
you to obey it if you will.

A comparison of these peculiar conditional constructions (491) expressing
hope or desire with clauses with mh/ expressing anxiety and desire to prevent a result, both
depending on oi)=da or

With

332 and

PLAT. Phaed.

w)=si kio/ntes
(366). This

ge/nhtai means to know (or see) the chances of
gaining this (object of desire); while ei)de/nai (or i)dei=n) mh\ tou=to ge/nhtai means to
know (or see) some way to prevent this (object of fear). The idea of
desire or anxiety belongs to the dependent clause, and not at all to the
leading verb.

§493

These Homeric expressions (491), in which nearly all the force is in the
protasis, so that the apodosis is not only suppressed but hardly felt at
all, helps to show how the particle ei) came to be an indirect interrogative, in the sense of
whether. But in Attic Greek, where the
interrogative use is fully established, only the simple ei) (never h)/n or e)a/n) can mean whether, even
when the verb is subjunctive (680).

[section 103]

## Mixed Constructions.

§498

The forms of protasis and apodosis which are contained in the
classification above (388-397) include by far the greater number of the
examples found in the classic authors. Many cases remain, however, in
which the protasis and apodosis do not belong to the same form.
Especially, the great wealth of conditional expressions which the
Homeric language exhibits in both protasis and apodosis (399) allowed great
variety of combination; and the early poets used much greater freedom in
these sentences than suited the more exact style of Attic prose.

[section 104]

## I. Optative in Protasis, with Future or Present Indicative
or an equivalent form in Apodosis.

§499

protasis with the optative is not infrequently followed by an apodosis

§501

## V. Several Protases in one Sentence.

§510

Two or more protases, not co-ordinate, may belong to the same
sentence; but one always contains the leading condition, to which the
rest of the sentence (including the other conditions) is the conclusion.
Here several protases may belong to one apodosis; or the leading
condition may be followed by two subordinate conditions, each with its
own apodosis. E.g. *kai\ ga\r a)\n
ou(=to/s ti pa/qh|, taxe/ws u(mei=s e(/teron *fi/lippon poih/sete,
a)/nper ou(/tw prose/xhte toi=s pra/gmasi to\n nou=n, for if anything shall happen to this Philip,
you will soon create another if this is your
way of attending to the business.

DEM. iv. 1; see

§511

It will be noticed that when the leading condition is unreal
(as in
EUR. Supp.
1084,
PLAT. Ap. 17 D, and
DEM. iv. 1, above), this makes all subordinate
past or present conditions also unreal, so far as the supposed case is
concerned, without regard to their own nature. Thus, in
DEM. iv. 1 and
xxxiii. 25 we have two directly opposite suppositions both stated as
contrary to fact, which could not be unless the leading supposition had
made the whole state of things supposed in the sentence unreal like
itself. It is obvious, therefore, that such a subordinate condition may
refer to a case which is not in itself
unreal, although it is part of a supposition which as a whole is unreal. This can be seen more easily in
English. We can say, if he had been an Athenian, he
would have been laughed at if he had talked as he did; but we
are far from implying that the latter supposition (the subordinate one)
is contrary to fact, although it would be expressed in Greek by ei) e)/legen. Still it is part
of a supposed unreal state of things. This explains an apparent
inconsistency in respect to sentences like ei)ko\s h)=n se tou=to paqei=n, you ought properly to have suffered this,
when the opposite of the infinitive is implied (415), the expression being
practically equivalent (as a conditional form) to tou=to e)/paqes a)\n ei) to\ ei)ko\s
e)/paqes. As tou=to
and to\ ei)ko/s are here
identical, the apodosis is denied in the denial of the protasis. But if
a new unreal protasis is added, the opposite of the infinitive is not
necessarily implied (see
422,
DEM.
1); and if we add a concessive protasis and say kai\ ei) mhde\n h)di/khsas, ei)ko\s
h)=n se tou=to paqei=n, even if you
had done nothing unjust, you
ought (still) to
have suffered this, tou=to generally represents what actually took place (see 422,
DEM. 2). Here a new
chief protasis has come in and changed the whole relation of the
apodosis to the sentence. This offers a satisfactory explanation of the
apparent anomaly in
SOPH. OT 221 , ou) ga\r
a)\n makra\n i)/xneuon au)to\s, mh\ ou)k e)/xwn ti
su/mbolon, where mh\ ou)k
e)/xwn is obviously equivalent to the condition ei) mh\ ei)=xon, while there is
yet no such opposite implied as but I have a
clue. The chief condition lies in the emphatic au)to/s, which is especially
forcible after ce/nos me/n
and ce/nos de/, and involves
ei) mo/nos i)/xneuon.
The meaning is, for I should not be very far on the
track, if I were attempting to trace it alone without a clue.
Thus without a clue becomes part of the
unreal supposition without being itself contrary to fact, while mh/ in mh\ ou)k
e)/xwn shows that e)/xwn is conditional, and not
merely descriptive (as if it were ou)k e)/xwn). For mh\
ou) with the participle, see 818.

[section 110]

## Section VII: Relative and Temporal Sentences.

§514

Relative sentences may be introduced by relative pronouns and
pronominal adjectives, or by relative adverbs of time, place, or manner. They
include therefore all temporal sentences.

Clauses introduced by e(/ws, pri/n, and other particles meaning until have many peculiarities, and are treated
separately (611-661).

§515

Relative sentences may be divided into two classes:—

First, those in which the antecedent of the relative is definite; that is, in which the relative
pronouns refer to definite persons or things, and the relative adverbs
to definite points of time, place, etc. Secondly, those in which the
antecedent is indefinite; that is, in which
no such definite persons, things, times, or places are referred to.

§516

Both the definite and the indefinite antecedent may be either
expressed or understood. E.g.

(Definite.) *tau=ta a(\
e)/xw o(ra=|s, you see these things
which I have; or a(\
e)/xw o(ra=|s. *(/ote e)bou/leto h)=lqen, (once) when he wished, he
came.

(Indefinite.) *pa/nta a(\
a)\n bou/lwntai e(/cousin, they will
have everything which they may want; or a(\ a)\n bou/lwntai e(/cousin, they will have whatever they may want.
*(/otan e)/lqh|, to/te tou=to
pra/cw, when he shall come (or
when he comes), then I will do this.
*(/ote bou/loito, tou=to
e)/prassen, whenever he wished,
he (always）
did this.
*(ws a)\n ei)/pw, ou(/tws
poiw=men, as I shall direct,
so let us act.

§517

The relative may be used to express a purpose
(565), or in a
causal sense (580). The antecedent may then be
either definite or indefinite.

§518

When the antecedent is indefinite, the negative of the
relative clause is mh/; when
it is definite, ou) is used
unless the general construction requires mh/ (as in prohibitions, wishes, final
expressions, etc.).

[section 112]

## Relative with Indefinite Antecedent. —Conditional
Relative.

§520

A relative with an indefinite
antecedent gives a conditional force to the clause in which it stands,
and is called a conditional relative. The
conditional relative clause stands in the relation of a protasis to the
antecedent clause, which is its apodosis (380). The negative particle is
mh/.

Thus, when we say a(\
nomi/zei tau=ta le/gei, he is saying
what he (actually) thinks, or a(\ e)no/mize tau=ta e)/legen, he
was saying what he thought, the actions of nomi/zei and e)no/mize are stated as actual
facts, occurring at definite times; but when we say a(\ a)\n nomi/zh| (tau=ta) le/gei, he (always) says whatever he
thinks, or a(\
nomi/zoi (tau=ta）
e)/legen, he (always）
said whatever he happened to be
thinking, nomi/zh|
and nomi/zoi do not state
any such definite facts, but rather what some one may think (or may have thought）
on any occasion on which he may speak or may
have spoken. So, when we say a(\
nomi/zei tau=ta le/cei, he will say
what he (now) thinks, nomi/zei denotes a fact; but when we say a(\ a)\n nomi/zh| le/cei,
he will say whatever he happens to be
(then) thinking, nomi/zh|
denotes a supposed future case. Again,—to take the case in which
the distinction is most liable to be overlooked,—when we say
a(\ ou)k oi)=da ou)k oi)/omai
ei)de/nai, what I do not
know, I do not think that I know,
ou)k oi)=da, as before,
denotes a simple fact, and its object a(/ has a definite antecedent; but when
Socrates says a(\ mh\ oi)=da ou)de\
oi)/omai ei)de/nai, the meaning is whatever I do not know (i.e. if there
is anything which I do not know), I do
not even think that I know it. In sentences like this, unless
a negative is used (518), it is often difficult to decide whether the antecedent is
definite or indefinite: thus a(\
oi)=da oi)/omai ei)de/nai may mean either what I (actually）
know, I think that I know, or whatever I know (if there
is anything which I know), I think that
I know it.

§521

The analogy of these indefinite relative clauses to
conditional sentences will be seen at once. The following examples will
make this clearer:—

*(/o ti bou/letai
dw/sw, I will give him whatever
he (now) wishes.
*ei)/ ti bou/letai, dw/sw,
if he wishes anything, I will give it. (402.)

*(/o ti e)bou/leto
e)/dwka a)/n, I should have given him
whatever he had wished.
*(/o ti mh\ e)ge/neto ou)k a)\n
ei)=pon, I should not have told what
had not happened.
*ei)/ ti e)bou/leto, e)/dwka
a)/n, if he had wished anything,
I should have given it.
*ei)/ ti mh\ e)ge/neto, ou)k a)\n
ei)=pon, I should not have told
anything if it had not happened. (410.)

*(/o ti a)\n bou/lhtai,
dw/sw, I will give him whatever he
shall wish.
*)ea/n ti bou/lhtai, dw/sw,
if he shall wish anything, I will give it. (444.)

*(/o ti bou/loito doi/hn
a)/n, I should give him whatever he
might wish.
*ei)/ ti bou/loito, doi/hn
a)/n, if he should wish anything,
I should give it. (455.)

*(/o ti a)\n bou/lhtai
di/dwmi, I (always) give him whatever

## I. Four Forms of Ordinary Conditional Relative Sentences.

§524

The conditional relative sentence has four forms, two of present and
past (525 and 528) and two of future conditions (529 and 531), which
correspond to the four forms of ordinary protasis.

## II. General Conditional Relative Sentences.

§532

A conditional relative sentence may express a general supposition, when the verb of the
antecedent clause denotes a customary or repeated action or a general
truth, while the relative clause refers in a general way to any act or acts of a given class. Here the
subjunctive with o(\s a)/n,
o(/tan, etc., follows primary tenses, and the optative (without
a)/n) follows secondary
tenses. (See 462.)
E.g. *)exqro\s ga/r moi kei=nos
o(mw=s *)ai+/dao pu/lh|sin, o(/s x' e(/teron me\n keu/qh| e)ni\
fresi\n, a)/llo de\ ei)/ph|, for that
man (i.e. any man) is hated by me like the very gates of Hades, who
conceals one thing in his mind and speaks another.

[section 123]

## Assimilation in Conditional Relative Clauses.

§558

When a conditional relative clause referring to the future depends on a subjunctive or optative
referring to the future, it regularly takes by assimilation the same
mood with its leading verb. The leading verb may be in a protasis or
apodosis, in another conditional relative clause, in an expression of a
wish, or in a final clause. E.g. *)ea/n tines oi(\ a)\n du/nwntai tou=to poiw=si, kalw=s
e(/cei, if any who shall be able do
this, it will be well.
*ei)/ tines oi(\ du/nainto tou=to
poioi=en, kalw=s a)\n e)/xoi, if any
who should be able should do this, it

makes oi(\ du/nainto after
an optative preferable to oi(\ a)\n
du/nwntai, which would express the same idea.) *teqnai/hn o(/te moi mhke/ti tau=ta
me/loi,

MIMN. i. 2.So in
Latin: Si absurde canat is qui se
haberi velit musicum, turpior
sit. — Sic
injurias fortunae quas ferre nequeas
defugiendo relinquas.

For examples see 529 and 531.

§559

When a conditional relative clause depends on a past tense of
the indicative implying the non-fulfilment of a condition, it regularly
takes a past tense of the indicative by assimilation. The leading verb may be in a protasis or
apodosis, in another conditional relative clause, in an expression of a
wish, or in a final clause. E.g. *ei)/ tines oi(\ e)du/nanto tou=to e)/pracan, kalw=s a)\n
e)/sxen, if any who had been able had
done this, it would have been well.
*ei)/qe pa/ntes oi(\ e)du/nanto
tou=to e)/pracan, O that all who had
been able had done this. So in Latin: Nam si solos eos diceres miseros quibus moriendum
esset, neminem tu quidem eorum qui
viverent exciperes.

For examples see 528.

§560

It will be seen that this principle of assimilation accounts
for the unreal indicative and the optative in conditional relative
sentences, which have been already explained by the analogy of the forms
of protasis. (See
528 and 531.) In fact, wherever this assimilation occurs, the
relative clause stands as a protasis to its antecedent clause.
Occasionally this principle is disregarded, so that a subjunctive
depends on an optative (178).

For the influence of assimilation in determining the mood of
a dependent sentence, see
176.

§561

The indicative in the construction of 525, referring simply
to the present or past, cannot be affected by assimilation, as this
would change its time. E.g. *(umei=s
d' e(/loisqe o(/ ti kai\ th=| po/lei kai\ a(/pasi sunoi/sein u(mi=n
me/llei,

and may you choose what is likely to benefit the
state and all of you.

sunene/gkoi, whatever you may
decide, may this be for our good.

SOPH.

e)/rdei would belong here; but o(\s ta/d' e)/rdoi (Laur.), =ei)/ tis ta/d' e)/rdoi, falls

In the last examples with mh/, the causal and the conditional forces are united, but

[section 127]

## Consecutive Clauses with w(/ste or
w(s and with e)f' w(=|
or e)f' w(=|te.

Consecutive Clauses with w(/ste or w(s and with e)f' w(=| or e)f' w(=|te. [note: See Gildersleeve in Jour. Phil. vii. pp. 161-175; and Seume, De Sententiis
Consecutivis Graecis, Göttingen, Phil. 1883.]

§582

A consecutive clause expresses a consequence, that is, the
effect or result (actual or potential) of something that is stated in
the leading clause. Such a clause is introduced by some relative word,
generally by w(/ste, so as, so that.
(See 575.) The
consequence may be either one which the action of the leading verb aims
at and tends to produce, or one which that
action actually does produce. This is the
fundamental distinction between w(/ste with the infinitive (with mh/ for its negative) and w(/ste with the indicative
(with ou) for its negative).
E.g. *pa=n poiou=sin w(/ste di/khn
mh\ dido/nai, they do everything in
such a way as (i.e. so as) not to suffer punishment, i.e. they aim, in all they do, at not being
punished; it is not, however, implied that they actually escape.

PLAT. Gorg.
479 C. On the other hand, pa=n poiou=sin w(/ste di/khn ou) dido/asin would mean they do everything in such a way that (i.e.
so that) they are
not punished.

§583

Though this illustrates the fundamental distinction in
thought on which the distinction in form is based, there are many
examples in which w(/ste
with the infinitive and w(/ste with the indicative seem to amount to essentially the
same thing, although the processes by which the meaning is expressed in
the two constructions are essentially different. Thus we can say ou(/tws e)sti\ deino\s w(/ste di/khn
mh\ dido/nai, he is so skilful as not
to be punished, and also ou(/tws e)sti\ deino\s w(/ste di/khn ou) di/dwsin, he is so skilful that he is not punished;
and though we should receive the same impression from both statements,
so that both might be made of the same man under the same circumstances,
yet the two constructions (one stating a tendency and the other a fact) are
very different, and they seemed far more so to a Greek than they do to
us.

§584

*(/wste is
properly a relative particle of comparison, meaning as. Its correlative so may be
expressed in a demonstrative like ou(/tws, or implied; as ou(/tws e)sti\ deino\s w(/ste se pei=sai, he is so skilful as to persuade you, or
h( po/lis tetei/xistai w(/ste
i(kanh\ ei)=nai sw/|zein tou\s e)noikou=ntas, the city is walled so as to be able to keep its
inhabitants safe. (See toiou/tous kai\ ou(/tw tre/fein ku/nas w(/ste
e)pixeirh=sai,
PLAT. Rep. 416 A; and compare toiou=tos oi(=os with the
infinitive in 759.) These expressions in Greek state no more than he has the skill to
persuade you and the city has walls
enough to be able, etc.; the further ideas that he does persuade and the
city is able are inferences, which are strongly suggested and
generally felt when the expressions are used, but they do not lie in the
words. When the Greek wishes to express these facts definitely and not
to leave them to inference, it uses the indicative with w(/ste; as ou(/tws e)sti\ deino\s w(/ste se pei/qei,
he is so skilful that he persuades
you, or h( po/lis
tetei/xistai w(/ste i(kanh/ e)stin. But here the use of a
finite verb compels the writer to make his expression more definite than
it was before; for, whereas w(/ste
pei=sai and w(/ste
i(kanh\ ei)=nai meant only (so）
as to persuade and (so) as to be able, without
limiting the expressions to past, present, or future time, he cannot use
a tense of the indicative without fixing its time, that is, without
making a definite statement. So long as the infinitive has no subject
and can be translated by our simple infinitive (as above), we can
generally express its force without putting into our translation more
than we find in the Greek; the formal distinction between so skilful as to persuade and so skilful that he persuades being apparent
even when we mean substantially the same by both. When the clause with
w(/ste is negative, a
marked distinction appears in Greek to show the different point of view
taken in the two expressions, and we have w(/ste mh\ pei=sai and w(/ste ou) pei/qei. This is of course lost
in English with our single negative. But when the infinitive has a
subject, it must be translated by a finite verb in some definite tense,
number, and person, that is, by a statement and not by a mere expression
of tendency, although the force of the infinitive in Greek is the same
as before. Thus we generally translate sxola/zeis, w(/ste qauma/zein e)me/ (
EUR. Hec. 730),
you delay, so that I am astonished, as
if it were w(/ste qauma/zw
e)gw/, simply because we cannot use our infinitive with a
subject expressed. If, however, we substitute an equivalent form which
avoids this difficulty, like so as to astonish
me, we see that there is really no such definite character in
w(/ste qauma/zein e)me/
as we impose upon it, and that it no more expresses a statement than
w(/ste se pei=sai
(above) does. The same difficulty of translating the Greek infinitive
with its subject has done much to obscure the force of the tenses of the
articular infinitive and of the infinitive with a)/n. (See also 603.)

In many uses of the infinitive with w(/ste it is not even inferred that the
result towards which the infinitive expresses a tendency is actually
reached. Thus, in clauses with w(/ste expressing a purpose or a condition, and where the
infinitive is generally used without w(/ste, we cannot substitute the indicative for the
infinitive (see the examples under 587, 2 and 3, and 588). [note: Shilleto (in the
Appendix to his edition of Demosthenes de Falsa
Legatione) thus illustrates the distinction between
w(/ste ou)k
e)bou/leto and w(/ste
mh\ bou/lesqai.
The difference seems simply to
be this: ou(/tws a)/frwn h(=n
w(/ste ou)k e)bou/leto, he was so
foolish that he did not wish (expressive of the real result or consequence); ou(/tws a)/frwn h)=n w(/ste mh\
bou/lesqai, he was so foolish as
not to wish (expressive of the natural consequence). . . . Now it is obvious that an
energetic speaker, wishing to express that the result (was not only
of a nature to follow, but) actually did follow, would employ the
indicative: whereas in ordinary and
unimpassioned language the infinitive
would imply all that was necessary, the
natural consequence supposing the
real.]

§585

In Homer w(/ste
(or rather w(/s te) is
found, with two exceptions (589), only in the sense of as, like w(/sper. See its use in similes, as w(/s te le/wn e)xa/rh,
Il. iii.
23.The te here is
like that commonly added to relatives in Homer (as in o(/s te) and to e)pei/ in Herodotus. The Attic
poets are the first to use w(/ste freely with the infinitive. In Sophocles we first find
w(/ste with the finite
moods; this seems to have arisen from a desire to express definitely the
accomplishment of the result, which the infinitive expressed only by
inference.

*(ws, originally
of the same meaning with w(/s
te, was seldom used in consecutive sentences except in certain

prefixed to it. It is important here to remember that w(/ste means only as (or, including the antecedent, so as); never so
that, except in the construction with the finite moods, although

§599

The examples in 598 have one common character: in all of them
the thought could be expressed equally well by w(/ste with the infinitive or w(/ste with a finite verb, for
even in
EUR. Ph.
1357 and DEM. liii. 1 a fact rather than a mere tendency is
expressed. We can, therefore, easily suppose a mixture of two
constructions by which, for example in
EUR. Hel. 107, instead of w(/ste mh\ ei)=nai or w(/ste ou)k e)/stin, either of
which would express the sense, we have w(/ste ou)k ei)=nai. [note: The explanation of
w(/ste ou) with the
infinitive on the ground of oratio obliqua was first made, I
believe, by Shilleto in the Appendix to his Demosthenes de Falsa Legatione
(1844). It is also given by
Madvig ( Synt.§ 205, Anm. 3), who confines w(/ste ou) to clauses depending on the
infinitive of oratio obliqua after verbs like fhmi/, oi)=mai, etc. (i.e. like the examples in 594).
Shilleto's faith in his own explanation was somewhat shaken by
finding that four of the passages quoted in 598 could not be brought
under his canon. Under the influence of Shilleto's essay, I
originally suggested the mixture of two equivalent constructions
given above, as applicable to all cases of w(/ste ou), not appreciating the wide
influence of the principle of oratio obliqua upon the
construction.] This occasional confusion would be made easier by
familiarity with w(/ste ou)
and the infinitive in indirect discourse.

[section 133]

## Temporal Particles signifying Until and Before.: e(/ws, o)/fra, ei)s o(/ or
ei)so/ke, e)/ste, a)/xri, me/xri, until.

Temporal Particles signifying Until and Before.: e(/ws, [note: In Homer, where the
form e(/ws would seldom suit
the verse, ei)/ws or ei)=os is commonly written.] o)/fra, ei)s o(/ or
ei)so/ke, e)/ste, a)/xri,
me/xri, until.

§611

All of these words are used also in the sense of while, so long as, and have the constructions
of ordinary relative clauses (514). In common with dum, donec, and quoad in Latin, and while or whiles in Elizabethan
English, [note:
He shall conceal it whiles (= until) you are
willing it shall come to note. Shakespeare. Twelfth Night, iv. 3.] they mean not
only during the time when, but also up to the time when. As relatives, in the
former sense they can have an antecedent like te/ws, so
long, e(/ws etc.
meaning as; in the latter sense they can
have one like me/xri
tou/tou, down to that time,
e(/ws etc. supplementing
this by at which or when. The idea of a clause with until is that the action (or negation) of the leading clause
continues to a time at which that of the
dependent clause takes place. That the former action then ceases is an inference generally made, but not
positively implied in the language, and not necessary. Our word until thus includes what the Greek may express
by me/xri tou/tou e(/ws or
(omitting the antecedent) by e(/ws alone.

*te/ws is
occasionally used like e(/ws, as in
DEM. xxi. 16.

§612

A clause with until referring to
an actual past occurrence (613) is simply a temporal clause of this peculiar character,
with the construction of a relative clause with a definite antecedent
(519). But when
it refers to the future, it becomes a conditional relative clause, and
maxou=mai e(/ws a)\n th\n po/lin
e(/lw, I shall (continue to) fight to the
time at which I shall take the city, has the conditional
force which comes from the indefinite antecedent; for even if me/xri tou/tou were inserted
here, it would denote no definite period, but only one limited or conditioned by the future capture of the city.
The actual apodosis to the condition is not maxou=mai alone, but rather the whole
implied idea, I shall go on fighting to the
future time, the limit of which is set by e(/ws a)\n e(/lw. It has been seen (486; 490) that ordinary
conditional clauses may condition not their expressed leading clause,
but one which the context implies; as cummaxi/an poiou=men, h)/n tis e)f' h(ma=s
i)/h|, we are making an alliance,
(to be ready) in case any one shall attack
us. Again, a conditional clause may refer to an object which is
aimed at in the action of the leading verb; as *pa/troklon e)/fepe i(/ppous, ei)/ ke/n min
e(/lh|s, turn your horses on P.,
if haply you may take him, i.e. that you may take him, if haply you may (487,
1). In like manner a conditional relative clause with until is very apt to refer to an object aimed
at, and thus to become at once final, relative, and conditional: thus in

Il. iii.
291 (see
613,
Il.
3), it is distinctly implied that the end of
the war (te/los
pole/moio) is a condition which is to limit the time of
fighting, and also an object at which the fighting aims. The same is
true in general of the other forms of conditional relative sentence
which the clause with until may take. It
will be seen (614,
Il.
2) that in the Odyssey e(/ws develops a peculiar force in this direction, which
makes it almost a final particle.

[section 134]

## pri/n,
before, until: Meaning and General Use of pri/n.

pri/n,
before, until [note: Geschichtliche Entwickelung der
Constructionen mit *pri/n, von Josef Sturm: Heft 3 of Schanz's Beiträge.] : Meaning
and General Use of pri/n.

§621

*pri/n was
originally a comparative adverb (= pro/teron and pa/ros), formed from pro/ and meaning before. It appears
in the usual adverbial relations; as pri/n moi u(pe/sxeto, he once
promised me;
pri\n w)/n, having been of old;
e)n tw=| pri\n xro/nw|,
in the former time; and it once takes
the genitive like a preposition in
PIND. Py. iv. 43, pri\n w(/ras, before
its time. With the infinitive it originally expressed a
simple temporal relation, pri\n
e)lqei=n being the equivalent of the later pro\ tou= e)lqei=n, before going. With the finite moods pri/n always expresses a limit of time and means until, like e(/ws, having become a conjunction, not losing, however, its
original meaning of before. From this
original comparative meaning, pri/n has a negative force, implying that something does or
does not happen before (i.e. in the absence of) another event; so that
ou)/pw or mh/pw with a temporal
participle may generally be substituted for pri/n and the infinitive. Thus, in nai=e de\ *ph/daion pri\n e)lqei=n
ui(=as *)axaiw=n,
Il. xiii. 172, for pri\n e)lqei=n, before they came, we could substitute ou)/pw e)lqo/ntwn, etc. So pri\n a)/n with the subjunctive
is often interchangeable with h)\n
mh/, and always implies it; thus mh\ a)pe/lqh|s pri\n a)\n a)kou/sh|s, do not depart until you hear, implies h)\n mh\ a)kou/sh|s, without hearing. One result of this negative
character of pri/n is its
strong affinity for the aorist, the tense which denotes simple occurrence. (See Jour.
Phil. ii. pp. 466 ff.)

§622

In Homeric Greek pri/n generally takes the primitive construction with the
infinitive without regard to the nature of the leading verb. In lyric
poetry, Herodotus, and Attic Greek, pri/n takes the infinitive chiefly when the leading clause
is affirmative; otherwise, it takes one of the finite moods, like e(/ws, having the sense of
until. But, while the indicative may
sometimes follow pri/n,
meaning until, when the leading clause is
affirmative, the subjunctive and optative are never used unless the
leading clause is negative or involves a negative idea.

[section 135]

## Development of the Constructions with pri/n.

§623

The Attic uses of pri/n with the indicative, subjunctive, and optative, are seen
in a primitive stage of development in Homer. The construction of pri/n itself with the
indicative was yet unknown; but four cases of pri/n g' o(/te with the indicative show a
tendency in this direction. Six cases of pri/n (without a)/n or ke/) with the subjunctive and one with the optative (in
indirect discourse) mark the beginning of the later usage with these
moods. On the other hand, 81 cases of pri/n with the infinitive show the
prevailing Homeric construction. Here, as in all periods of the
language, when pri/n takes
the infinitive, we have simply a statement of fact, that one thing
precedes another; in nai=e de\
*ph/daion pri\n e)lqei=n ui(=as *)axaiw=n, and he dwelt in Pedaeum before the coming of the
sons of the Greeks, pri\n e)lqei=n implies no more than pro\ a)fi/cews or the later pro\ tou= e)lqei=n. Any further
idea that may be implied comes from the context, and is not found in the
words. This use of pri/n has
little analogy in Greek syntax, its nearest parallel being the later use
of w(/ste or w(s with the infinitive. The
simplest theory, which best suits the Homeric usage, seems to be that
pri/n has a

quasi-prepositional relation to the infinitive, which is a
verbal noun, a relation the same in effect as that of pro/ in pro\ tou= e)lqei=n in the later Attic
construction. (See
XEN. Mem. ii. 6, 6 , and
DEM. xix. 73.) A similar use of a)nti/ with the infinitive in a
few cases in Herodotus (see 803) shows a tendency to go further in the
same direction.

§624

The Homeric language was generally contented with the simple
pri/n and the
infinitive, even when it was implied that the clause with pri/n set a limit to the action
(or negation) of the leading clause, i.e. when pri/n could be expressed by until. So in
Il. xxi. 100, pri\n *pa/troklon e)pispei=n ai)/simon h)=mar,
to/fra ti/ moi pefide/sqai fi/lteron h)=en *trw/wn, i.e.
until the death of Patroclus I preferred to
spare the Trojans (which he will no longer do); and xix. 312,
ou)de/ ti qumw=| te/rpeto pri\n
pole/mou sto/ma du/menai, i.e. he felt
no pleasure until he entered the battle; in both cases the
Attic Greek might have used pri/n with the indicative. So also when the clause with pri/n is future and
conditional; as in
Il. xix. 423, ou) lh/cw pri\n *trw=as a)/dhn e)la/sai
pole/moio, I will not stop until I have
given the Trojans enough of war. It was in cases like the
last, where the mere temporal pri\n
e)la/sai expresses the future condition very imperfectly,
that the need of a more exact form was first felt. The need existed only
after negative sentences, as here only could such a future condition be
expressed by pri/n
consistently with its original meaning before. I
shall not cease fighting until (before) I see the end of the war
contains a future condition (= h)\n
mh/) which pri/n
can properly express; but the equivalent affirmative, I shall go on fighting until I see the end of the
war, could not be expressed by pri/n, as we cannot substitute before for until,
but it would require e(/ws,
which is until with no sense of before. The forms of parataxis suggested a
simple and natural way of meeting this want, through the adverbial use
of pri/n. In a sentence like
ou)de/ min a)nsth/seis: pri\n
kai\ kako\n a)/llo pa/qh|sqa, nor
will you recall him to life:—sooner than this will you suffer
some new affliction,
Il. xxiv. 551, we have only to remove the
colon and make pri/n a
conjunction to obtain the regular construction of pri/n with the subjunctive, nor will you recall him to life before (until) you suffer some
new affliction. This result could not have been attained with
an affirmative leading clause; for while ou) tou=to poih/sw: pri/n me keleu/sh|s,
I shall not do this:—you shall command
me first, gives the meaning I shall not
do this before you command me, the paratactic affirmative,
tou=to poih/sw: pri/n me
keleu/sh|s, would give only you will
command me before I do this. I shall do this before you command
me would be tou=to poih/sw
pri/n se keleu=sai, which is not the result of any form of
parataxis. The six cases of pri/n with the subjunctive in Homer are all without a)/n or ke/, and all follow negatives. The primitive
character and the rarity of this construction seem to show that we are
nearer the original parataxis here than in any other form; while the
change of the subjunctive to the optative after a past tense in
Il. xxi. 580
(see 639) shows that the dependence of the clause with pri/n is thoroughly established
(cf. 307). An attempt to arrive at the same result in a more awkward way
appears in two cases of pri/n g'
o(/t' a)/n with the subjunctive in the Odyssey (641), where pri/n introduces the
subjunctive with o(/t' a)/n
very much as it introduces the infinitive.

§625

No case of pri/n
with the indicative occurs in Homer; but the want was supplied by pri/n g' o(/te dh/ with the
indicative, which resembles pri/n g'
o(/t' a)/n with the subjunctive just mentioned. As this
construction is not the result of parataxis, and there is no such
obstacle to combining the ideas of until and
before in statements of past fact after
affirmative clauses as was felt in future conditions (624), we find pri/n g' o(/te with the indicative after
both affirmative and negative sentences (see the examples in 636). It
thus appears that pri/n was
not sufficiently established as a conjunction in Homer to take the
indicative without the intervention of o(/te, although pri/n with the subjunctive had become a
fixed construction.

The history of the uses of pri/n after Homer will be found below. (See
627; 632-634; 637; 642; 643; 645.)

（Prose.) In Attic prose and in

[section 138]

## pri/n
with the Subjunctive and Optative: Subjunctive.

§638

When a clause with pri/n, until, refers to the
future, and depends on a negative clause of
future time (not containing an optative), pri/n takes the subjunctive, like e(/ws in a similar case (613,
3).

§639

In Homer pri/n
does not take ke/ or a)/n with the subjunctive, the
form of the original parataxis being still retained (624). The examples of the
subjunctive are these:—

*ou) ga/r pw
katadu/someq' ei)s *)ai/dao do/mous, pri\n mo/rsimon h)=mar
e)pe/lqh|, we shall not yet descend
to the house of Hades, until the fated
day shall come.

Od. x.
174. (Here, if we insert a colon after do/mous and take pri/n as an adverb, sooner than this, we have the paratactic form.) So
Il. xviii.
135;
Od.
xiii. 335,
Od. xvii. 7.In
Il. xviii. 190, ou)/ me pri/n g' ei)/a qwrh/ssesqai,
pri/n g' au)th\n i)/dwmai, she did
not permit me to arm myself until I should see her, the
subjunctive of direct discourse (seen in xviii. 135) is retained after a
past tense. So
Il. xxiv. 781.In
Il. xxi. 580 a similar subjunctive has been
changed to the optative (644).

§640

Hesiod has two cases of pri/n with the subjunctive,
Th. 222,
Op. 738, still without ke/ or a)/n as in Homer. *pri\n a)/n first occurs in THEOGN. 963 (see
642).

§641

Two cases of pri/n g'
o(/t' a)/n (used like pri/n) with the subjunctive occur in the Odyssey. The first
is especially instructive, ii. 373: a)ll' o)/moson mh\ mhtri\ fi/lh| ta/de muqh/sasqai, pri/n g' o(/t'
a)\n e(ndeka/th te duwdeka/th te ge/nhtai, h)\ au)th\n poqe/sai kai\
a)formhqe/ntos a)kou=sai, but swear
not to tell this to my mother until the eleventh or twelfth day
shall come, or (until) she shall miss me
and hear of my departure. Here pri/n first introduces o(/t' a)\n ge/nhtai and then the two
infinitives, having the same prepositional force with both. But in iv.
746, where the same scene is described, we have e)meu= d' e(/leto me/gan o(/rkon, mh\ pri\n soi\
e)re/ein pri\n dwdeka/thn ge gene/sqai h)\ s' au)th\n poqe/sai kai\
a)formhqe/ntos a)kou=sai, the simpler and more common pri\n gene/sqai taking the
place of the unwieldy pri/n g' o(/t'
a)\n ge/nhtai. The other case is iv. 475: ou) pri\n moi=ra fi/lous i)de/ein,
pri/n g' o(/t' a)\n *ai)gu/ptoio u(/dwr e)/lqh|s.

## Optative.

§643

When a clause with pri/n, until, referring to the
future, depends on a negative clause containing an optative in protasis
or apodosis, in a wish, or in a final clause, it may have the optative
(without a)/n) by
assimilation, like a conditional relative clause (613, 4), or it may
take the infinitive. These cases of the optative occur:—

*ou) ga\r a)\n ei)dei/hs
a)ndro\s no/on ou)de\ gunaiko\s, pri\n peirhqei/hs,

for you cannot know the mind of a man or a woman
until you have tested it.

[section 143]

## Section VIII: Indirect Discourse or Oratio Obliqua,
including Indirect Quotations and Questions.

§662

The words or thoughts of any person may be quoted either
directly or indirectly. A direct quotation is one which gives the exact
words of the original speaker or writer. An indirect quotation is one in
which the original words conform to the construction of the sentence in
which they are quoted. Thus the expression tau=ta bou/lomai may be quoted either
directly (in oratio recta), as le/gei tis
tau=ta
bou/lomai; or indirectly (in oratio
obliqua), as le/gei tis
o(/ti tau=ta bou/letai or fhsi/ tis tau=ta bou/lesqai, some one says that he wishes for these.

§663

Indirect quotations may be introduced by o(/ti or w(s and occasionally by other particles (negatively o(/ti ou), w(s ou), etc.) with
a finite verb; sometimes by the infinitive without a particle; sometimes
also by the participle.

1. *(/oti, that, was originally the neuter relative
o(/ ti, used as a
limiting accusative, in respect to which (or
what), as to which,
how far, etc. In Homer o(/, neuter of the relative o(/s, is used like o(/ti (709, 1). Thus oi)=da o(/ ti (or o(\) kaka\ mh/detai at first meant I know
as to what he plans evil, or I know
about his planning evil, and afterwards came to mean I know that he plans evil.

2. *(ws, the
relative adverb of manner (312, 1), in this construction originally
meant in what manner, how; and afterwards
became established in the same sense as o(/ti, that.
Compare the German use of wie (how) in narration. How for that is heard in vulgar
English (as I told him how I saw this), and
how that was once in good use in this
sense for that.
*(/opws is sometimes used
like w(s in indirect
discourse (706).

3. By a use similar to that of w(s
(2), ou(/neka and o(qou/neka are sometimes
weakened from their meaning for which purpose,
wherefore, to the same sense as o(/ti and w(s, that
(710, 1). These words are also used in a causal sense, because, like o(/ti, o(/, and w(s
(712).

On the other hand, dio/ti, because, sometimes has
the sense of o(/ti, that (710, 2).

4. *(/ote, when, in Homer sometimes loses its temporal
force, and approaches o(/ti
in meaning (709, 3).

§664

1. Indirect quotations with o(/ti, w(s, etc., form the chief part of the
class of substantive sentences, in which an
assertion introduced by one of these particles is the subject or the
object of a verb. But these sentences have no peculiar construction,
except after verbs implying thought or the expression of thought
(verba sentiendi et
declarandi), as they elsewhere have the simple indicative or
any other form which would be used in the corresponding independent
assertions. See ou)x a(/lis w(s
e)kei/rete kth/mat' e)ma/,

is it not enough that you wasted my property?

Od. ii.
312; polu\ ke/rdion e)/pleto
o(/tti u(po/eicen,
Il. xv. 227; tou=to a)/cion e)painei=n, o(/ti to\n fo/bon
die/lusan tw=n *(ellh/nwn
(668),
PLAT. Menex. 241
B; tou=t' a)dikei=, o(/ti
a)xrei=on th\n e)piei/keian kaqi/sthsin,
DEM. xx. 155.

2. The infinitive of indirect discourse belongs to the large
class of subject and object infinitives (745; 746; 751), being
distinguished from the others of this class by preserving the time of
its tense from the finite verb which it represents (85; 667, 3). [note: See Schmitt,
Ueber den Ursprung des Substantivsatzes mit
Relativpartikeln im Griechischen, in Schanz's Beiträge, Heft 8.]

§665

1. Indirect questions may be introduced by ei), whether (rarely by a)=ra), and also by interrogative pronouns, pronominal
adjectives, and adverbs, and by most relatives. Alternative indirect
questions may be introduced by po/teron (po/tera) . . . h)/, ei)/te
. . . ei)/te, ei) . . . h)/, ei) . . . ei)/te, whether . . . or.

*)ea/n or h)/n never means whether (see 493).

2. In Homer single indirect questions (when they are not
introduced by interrogatives) generally have h)/ or ei), whether; and
alternative questions have h)/ (h)e/) . . .
h)= (h)=e), sometimes ei)/ te . . . ei)/ te, whether . . . or.

Bekker never allows ei) or ei)/ te in
indirect questions in Homer, always writing h)/ or h)/ te, without regard to the MSS.

3. Indirect questions follow the same principles as indirect
quotations with o(/ti or
w(s, in regard to their
moods and tenses. (For examples, see 669.)

§666

The term indirect discourse or
oratio obliqua includes all clauses
which express indirectly the words or thoughts of any person (including
those of the speaker himself), after verbs which imply thought or the
expression of thought (verba sentiendi et
declarandi), and after such expressions as fai/netai, it appears, dokei=, it
seems, dh=lo/n
e)stin, it is evident, safe/s e)stin, etc.

The term may be further applied to any single dependent
clause, in any sentence, which indirectly expresses the thought of any
other person than the speaker (or past thoughts of the speaker himself),
even when the preceding or following clauses are not in indirect
discourse. (See 694
and 684.)

[section 144]

## General Principles of Indirect Discourse.

§667

The following are the general principles of indirect
discourse, the particular applications of which are shown in 669710.

1. In indirect quotations after o(/ti or w(s and in indirect questions,

（a) after primary tenses, each
verb retains both the mood and the tense of the direct discourse, no
change being made except (when necessary) in the person of the verb;

（b) after secondary tenses, each
primary tense of the indicative and each subjunctive of the direct
discourse may be either changed to the same tense of the optative or
retained in its original mood and tense. The imperfect and pluperfect,
having no tenses in the optative, are generally retained in the
indicative (but see 673). An aorist indicative belonging to a dependent clause of the direct discourse
remains unchanged, but one belonging to the leading clause may be
changed to the optative like a primary tense.

2. Secondary tenses of the indicative expressing an unreal
condition, indicatives with a)/n, and all optatives (with or without a)/n), are retained, with no change in
either mood or tense, after both primary and secondary tenses.

3. When the quotation depends on a verb which takes the
infinitive or participle, the leading verb of the quotation is changed
to the corresponding tense of the infinitive
or participle, after both primary and secondary tenses, a)/n being retained if it is in
the direct form; and the dependent verbs follow the preceding rules.

4. The adverb a)/n is never joined with a verb in indirect discourse unless
it stood also in the direct form. On the other hand, a)/n is never omitted in indirect discourse
if it was used in the direct form; except that, when it is joined to a
relative word or a particle before a subjunctive in direct discourse, it
is regularly dropped when the subjunctive is changed to the optative
after a past tense in indirect discourse.

5. The indirect discourse regularly retains the same negative
particle which would be used in the direct form. But the infinitive and
participle sometimes take mh/ in indirect discourse where ou) would be used in the direct form. (See
examples under 685 and 688.) In indirect questions introduced by ei), whether, and in the second part of alternative indirect
questions (665),
mh/ can be used as well
as ou).

§668

As an indirect quotation or question is generally the object
or subject of its leading verb, it may stand in apposition with a
pronoun like tou=to which
represents such an object or subject; as tou=to le/gomen, o(/ti sofo/s e)stin, we say this, that he is
wise;
tou=to dh=lo/n e)stin, o(/ti sofo/s
e)stin, this is plain, that he is wise;
tou=to skeyo/meqa, ei) a)lhqh=
le/geis, we shall inquire into
this, whether you tell the
truth.

[section 145]

§670

（a) After past tenses the
indicative and optative are in equally good use; the optative being used
when the writer incorporates the quotation entirely into his own
sentence, and the indicative when he quotes it in the original words as
far as his own construction allows. The indicative here, like the
subjunctive in final clauses after past tenses (318), is merely a more vivid form
of expression than the optative, with no difference in meaning. We even
find both moods in the same sentence. E.g. *ou(=toi e)/legon o(/ti *ku=ros me\n te/qnhken,
*)ariai=os de\ pefeugw\s e)n tw=| staqmw=| ei)/h kai\ le/goi, k.t.l.

XEN. An. ii. 1,
3. (Here te/qnhken contains the most important part of the message.)
*)ek de\ tou/tou e)punqa/neto
h)/dh au)tw=n kai\ o(po/shn o(do\n dih/lasan, kai\ ei) oi)koi=to h(
xw/ra.
Id. Cyr. iv. 4,

*)eto/lma le/gein, w(s xre/a te
pa/mpolla e)kte/tiken u(pe\r e)mou= kai\ w(s polla\ tw=n e)mw=n
la/boien.

（b) The perfect and future were
less familiar than the other tenses of the optative, so that these
tenses were sometimes retained in the indicative even when the present
or the aorist was changed to the optative. See the last two examples
under (a). In indirect questions the aorist indicative was generally retained (see
125). Some writers (as Thucydides) preferred the more direct forms in
all indirect discourse (320).

§671

In Homer this construction (669) is fully developed in indirect questions:
see examples of both indicative and optative in 669, 1 and 2. But in
indirect quotations, while the indicative is freely used after both
present and past tenses, the change of the indicative to the optative
after past tenses had not yet been introduced. In the single case of
ei)pei=n w(s with the
optative, mermh/rice . . e(/kasta
ei)pei=n, w(s e)/lqoi kai\ i(/koit' e)s patri/da gai=an,
he hesitated about telling him each
event, how he had returned, etc.,

Od. xxiv.
237, w(s appears only
on its way from its meaning how (663,
Od. 2) to its
later use with the optative as that. We
first find the optative in genuine oratio obliqua (with w(s) Hymn.
Ven. 214, ei)=pen w(s e)/oi. Further, the later
principle by which the indicative after past tenses (when it is not
changed to the optative) retains the tense
of the direct form is almost unknown in the Homeric language. Here a
present or perfect indicative of the direct discourse after a past tense
is changed to an imperfect or pluperfect; so that I
knew that he was planning evil, which in Attic would be
e)gi/gnwskon o(/ti kaka\
mh/doito (or mh/detai), in Homer is gi/gnwskon o(/ (= o(/ti) kaka\
mh/deto,
Hom. Od. iii. 166. (For examples, see 674.) The aorist indicative,
which has no corresponding tense to express its own time referred to the
past, was always retained after past tenses; as in gnw= o(/ oi( ou)/ti h)=lqen,
Hom. Il. xi.
439; so i. 537,
Hom. Il. xxii. 445.Likewise the future
indicative is once retained, in
Hom. Od. xiii. 340, h)/|de) o(\ nosth/seis, I knew that you would return; but elsewhere
the past future with e)/mellon is used, as in
Hom. Il. xx. 466, ou)de\ to\ h)/|dh o(\ ou) pei/sesqai
e)/mellen, and
Hom. Od. xix. 94,
Hom. Il. xi. 22.These examples
show the need of the later future optative (129). In
Hom. Il. xxii.
10, ou)de/ nu/ pw/ me e)/gnws
w(s qeo/s ei)mi, and xx. 265 the present expresses a present
truth rather than a past fact.

It thus appears that the peculiar constructions with o(/ti and w(s in oratio obliqua (667, 1, b), which gave such grace and variety to the
later language, were not yet developed in Homer; but clauses with o(/ti, w(s, etc., were still
connected with the leading verb by the same looser construction which we
use in English (as I knew that he was planning
evil), the dependent verb expressing its own absolute time (see
22), as it did in the relative clauses in which these clauses
originated, or in the more primitive parataxis. Thus gi/gnwskon o(\ kaka\ mh/deto (above) meant
originally I knew as to what he was planning
evil; and without o(/, in a still earlier stage, I knew: he
was planning evil (which we can say in English). Even after
the more thorough incorporation of the dependent clause was established,
by which either mh/detai or
mh/doito became the
regular form, the more primitive imperfect is occasionally found, even
in Attic prose (see
674, 2).

The most common Homeric construction in indirect discourse is
that of fhmi/ with the
infinitive, of which 130 examples occur. [note: See Schmitt, Ursprung des Substantivsatzes, p. 70. The following

## Infinitive in Indirect Discourse.

§683

When the infinitive stands in indirect discourse, its tense
represents the corresponding tense of the finite verb in the direct
form, the present and perfect including the imperfect and pluperfect. If
a)/n was used in the
direct form, it must be retained in the quotation, each tense with
a)/n representing the
corresponding tenses of either indicative or optative with a)/n. E.g. *fhsi\ gra/fein, he
says that he is writing;
e)/fh gra/fein, he said that he was writing;
fh/sei gra/fein, he will say that he is (then) writing. (He says gra/fw.) *fhsi\ (e)/fh) gra/fein a)\n,
ei) e)du/nato, he says (or
said) that he
should now be writing, if he were able. (He says e)/grafon a)/n.) *fhsi\ (e)/fh) gra/fein a)\n, ei) du/naito, he
says (or said) that he should write, if he should (ever) be able. (He says gra/foimi a)/n.)

*fhsi\ gra/yai,
he says that he wrote;
e)/fh gra/yai, he said that he had written;
fh/sei gra/yai, he will say that he wrote. (He says e)/graya.) *fhsi\ (e)/fh) gra/yai a)\n,
ei) e)dunh/qh, he says (or
said) that he
should have written, if he had been able. (He says e)/graya a)/n.) *fhsi\ (e)/fh) gra/yai a)\n, ei) dunhqei/h, he
says (or said) that he should write, if he should (ever) be able. (He says gra/yaimi a)/n.)

*fhsi\ (fh/sei) gegrafe/nai, he
says (or will say) that he has written;
e)/fh gegrafe/nai, he said that he had written. (He says ge/grafa.) For the perfect with
a)/n, see below and 206.

*fhsi\ (fh/sei) gra/yein, he
says (or will say) that he will write;
e)/fh gra/yein, he said that he would write. (He says gra/yw.)

§684

The infinitive is said to stand in
indirect discourse and its tenses correspond to those of the
indicative or optative, when it depends on a verb implying thought or
the expression of thought (one of the class of verba sentiendi et declarandi), and when also the thought, as originally conceived,
would have been expressed by some tense of the indicative (with or
without a)/n) or optative
(with a)/n), so that it can
be transferred without change of tense to the infinitive. Thus in bou/letai e)lqei=n, he wishes to go, e)lqei=n represents no form of either aorist
indicative or aorist optative, and is therefore said to be not in
indirect discourse. But in fhsi\n
e)lqei=n, he says that he
went, e)lqei=n
represents h)=lqon of the
direct discourse. The distinction in the time of the infinitive
(especially of the aorist infinitive) in these two uses is obvious.

It may be asked why the infinitive after certain other verbs
should not be said to stand in indirect discourse; for example, why in
keleu/ei se e)lqei=n or
mh\ e)lqei=n we should
not say that e)lqei=n
represents e)lqe/ or mh\ e)/lqh|s of direct
discourse. This might perhaps be done; and we might possibly make e)lqei=n in bou/lomai e)lqei=n represent e)/lqoimi, may I go. But with other verbs of the same
class, as those of advising, teaching, striving,
choosing, no form of direct discourse can even be imagined.
It is much harder to draw a line between these last verbs and verbs like
keleu/w and bou/lomai, or even between
these two, than where it is drawn above. It is impossible to say where a
Greek would have drawn the line, or to be sure that he would have drawn
any line at all; for our own use, the usual definition of the infinitive
in oratio obliqua (as given above) is certainly the most convenient.

§685

（*mh/, with Infinitive.) The negative particle of
the infinitive in indirect discourse is regularly ou), which is retained from the direct form
(667, 5). But, after certain verbs which belong to the intermediate
class between those which take the infinitive in indirect discourse and
those which do not (see 136), the infinitive regularly takes mh/ for its negative. Such are
verbs of hoping, promising, and swearing; with those signifying to agree or consent (o(mologw=),
to trust (pisteu/w), to be
persuaded (pe/peismai), to testify (marturw=). [note: See Liddell and
Scott, ed. 7, under mh/,
B. 5, C; also Gildersleeve in Jour.
Phil. i. p. 51.] The infinitive occasionally has
mh/ even after the verbs
which most regularly take the infinitive with ou) in indirect discourse, as fhmi/, le/gw, nomi/zw,
h(gou=mai, etc. E.g. *xrh=n

[section 150]

## Indirect Quotation of Complex Sentences.

§689

When a complex sentence is indirectly quoted, its leading
verb follows the principles already stated for simple sentences
(669-688).

1. If the quotation depends on a primary tense, all the
dependent verbs of the original sentence retain the mood and tense of
the direct discourse.

2. After a secondary tense, all dependent verbs of the
original sentence which there stood in the present, perfect, or future
indicative, or in any tense of the subjunctive, may either be changed to
the same tense of the optative or retain both the mood and tense of the
direct discourse, the optative being the more common form. When the
subjunctive is changed to the optative, a)/n is dropped, e)a/n, o(/tan, etc., becoming ei), o(/te, etc.

3. But dependent secondary tenses of the indicative and all
dependent optatives remain unchanged after all tenses (see, however,
693). E.g.

The aorist indicative is not changed to the aorist optative
here, to avoid confusion, as the latter tense in such dependent clauses
generally represents the aorist subjunctive of the direct form. Thus
e)/fh a(\ eu(/roi
dw/sein means he said that he would give
whatever he might find (a(\ a)\n eu(/rw dw/sw); but if a(\ eu(/roi could also represent a(\ eu(=ron, it might also mean
he said that he would give what he had
found. In the leading clause the ambiguity is confined to
indirect questions, in which the aorist indicative is generally retained
for the same reason (see 125).

e)/legen o(/ti xai/roi a)\n ei)

§690

The dependent verbs of a quotation may be changed to the
optative in indirect discourse, even when the leading verb retains the
indicative; and sometimes (though rarely) a dependent verb retains the
subjunctive or indicative, when the leading verb is changed to the
optative. This may give rise to a great variety of constructions in the
same sentence. E.g. *dhlw/sas o(/ti
e(/toimoi/ ei)si ma/xesqai ei)/ tis e)ce/rxoito.

1. (*(/etoimoi/ ei)sin
e)a/n tis e)ce/rxhtai.) *lu/sandros ei)=pe o(/ti paraspo/ndous u(ma=s e)/xoi, kai\ o(/ti

[section 151]

## Single Dependent Clauses in Indirect Discourse.

§694

1. The principles which govern dependent clauses of indirect
discourse (689)
apply also to all dependent clauses in sentences of every kind (even
when what precedes is not in indirect discourse), if such clauses
express indirectly the past thought of any
person, even that of the speaker himself. This affects the construction
only when the leading verb is past; then the dependent clause may either
take the optative, in the tense in which the
thought was originally conceived, or retain both the mood and the tense
of the direct discourse. When a subjunctive is changed to an optative,
a)/n is dropped.

2. Secondary tenses of the indicative here (as in 689, 3)
regularly remain unchanged. But an aorist indicative sometimes becomes
optative when no ambiguity can result from the change (see 693): this
may occur in causal sentences (699 and 714) and in the relative
sentences of 700.

The principle of 694 applies to the following
constructions:—

## Section IX: Causal Sentences.

§712

Causal sentences express the cause of something stated in the
leading sentence. They may be introduced by o(/ti, dio/ti or dio/per, w(s, ou(/neka or o(qou/neka, because; by e)pei/, e)peidh/, o(/te, o(po/te, eu)=te,
and sometimes o(/pou, since, seeing
that; and in Homer by o(/ or o(/ te
(o(/ t)), because.

negative particle is ou).

§715

We should suppose that in causal sentences of the latter
class (714) the
mood and tense by which the cause would be originally stated might also
be retained, as in ordinary indirect discourse; so that in
THUC. ii. 21,
above, for example, we might have o(/ti ou)k e)p eca/gei in the same sense as o(/ti ou)k e)peca/goi. This,
however, seems to have been avoided, to prevent the ambiguity which
might arise from the three forms, e)pech=gen, e)peca/goi, and e)peca/gei. It will be remembered that the
form e)pech=gen, which is
the most common in the expression of a past cause, is also the original
form for expressing the corresponding time in indirect discourse,
although it became exceptional here in the later usage (671; 674).

For causal relative sentences see 580. For the causal participle
see 838.

§719

1. A causal sentence may give the cause of something that is
implied, but not expressed, in the leading sentence. Especially it may
give the reason for making a statement, rather than for the fact stated.
In dialogues, a causal sentence may refer to an implied yes or no. E.g.

*ou)/ nu kai\ u(mi=n
oi)/koi e)/nesti go/os, o(/ti m' h)/lqete khdh/sontes;
have you now no mourning at home, that you have come to distress me? (i.e. I ask this, because you have come).

[section 156]

## Section X: Expression of a Wish.

§720

Wishes may be divided into two classes: (a) those referring to a future object, and (b) those referring to a present or past object
which (it is implied) is not or was not attained. To the former class
belong such wishes as O that he may come! or
O that this may happen!—Utinam
veniat, Utinam fiat; and to the latter, such as O
that this had happened! or O that this
were true!—Utinam hoc factum esset, Utinam hoc verum
esset.

From its use in wishes the optative mood (e)/gklisis
eu)ktikh/) received its name.

[section 157]

I. by the optative alone; as in ge/noito tou=to, may
this happen, mh\

II. by the optative with ei)/qe or ei)

§730

There are many passages in Homer in which it is open to doubt
whether the poet intended to express a wish with some form of ei), followed by a potential
optative in a new sentence, or to form a complete conditional sentence.
Such are—

*ei) ga\r e)p' a)rh=|sin
te/los h(mete/rh|si ge/noito: ou)k a)/n tis tou/twn ge e)u/qronon
*)hw= i(/koito.
Od. xvii. 496.
*ai)\ ga\r tou=to, cei=ne, e)/pos
tetelesme/non ei)/h: tw=| ke ta/xa gnoi/hs filo/thta/ te polla/ te
dw=ra e)c e)meu=.
Od. xv. 536.

If we keep the colon after ge/noito in the former passage, we may
translate, O that fulfilment may be granted our
prayers: not one of these would (then) see the fair-throned Dawn.
With a comma after ge/noito,
we may translate, if fulfilment should be granted
our prayers, not one of these would see the fair-throned
Dawn. So in the second passage we may translate, according to the
punctuation, O that this word may be accomplished:
then would you quickly be made aware of kindness and many gifts from
me;—or if this word should be
accomplished, you would then quickly be made aware, etc.
These are probably rightly punctuated above, especially the second; and
the wish is on the verge of independent existence, being almost ready to
dispense with the apodosis. The half-independent half-dependent nature
of such clauses is best seen in a case like the following, where ei) e)qe/loi is first stated as
an independent wish, and is afterwards repeated as the protasis of a
regular apodosis:—

*ei) ga/r s' w(\s
e)qe/loi file/ein glaukw=pis *)aqh/nh w(s to/t' *)odu/ssh=os
perikh/deto kudali/moio dh/mw| e)/ni *trw/wn, o(/qi pa/sxomen
a)/lge) *)axaioi/: . . . ei)/ s' ou(/tws e)qe/loi file/ein kh/doito/
te qumw=|, tw=| ke/n tis kei/nwn ge kai\ e)klela/qoito
ga/moio.
Od. iii. 217.

The meaning is, if only Athena would
love you as she then loved Ulysses; . . . if (I say) she would thus
love you, then would many a one (of the suitors) cease to think of marriage. Here, instead of
leaving a simple apodosis like the kalw=s a)\n e)/xoi of Aristarchus to be mentally supplied,
or to be felt without being actually supplied, the protasis is repeated
(as if by afterthought) and a more precise form of conclusion is then
actually expressed.

Such examples as the first two are sometimes adduced as
evidence that ei) with the
optative in protasis was originally a form of wish, to which an apodosis
was afterwards appended. For a discussion of this view, see Appendix
I.

## Wishes (Not Attained) in Present or Past Time.

§731

A wish referring to a present or past object, which (it is
implied) is not or was not attained, may be expressed in Greek in two
ways:—

I. by the past tenses of the indicative, used as in unreal
conditions, with ei)/qe or
ei) ga/r; or

II. by w)/felon,
aorist of o)fei/lw, owe, with the infinitive.

§732

I. The past tenses of the indicative with ei)/qe or ei) ga/r, in present and past wishes,
correspond to the optative with these particles in future wishes. The
construction was originally a protasis with its apodosis suppressed,
ei) ga/r me ei)=des
meaning, O if you had seen me! This form of
wish is common in the Attic writers, but is unknown to Homer (735).

The imperfect and aorist indicative are distinguished here as
in the unreal condition (410). E.g. *)iw\ ga=
ga=, ei)/q' e)/m' e)de/cw, O

received me.

§735

This form with w)/felon or w)/fellon is the only expression known to Homer for past wishes, the secondary tenses of the
indicative being not yet used in this construction, although they were
already in good use in past (though not in present) conditions (435). In present
wishes, Homer has the present optative (739) as well as the construction with w)/felon. (See 438.)

§736

seen to be analogous to e)/dei and xrh=n
with the infinitive, implying that what ought to
be or to have been does not or did
not happen. Only after its original meaning was obscured by familiar use
could ei)/qe or ei) ga/r have been prefixed to
it. *mh\ w)/felon may be
explained in the same way; or we may suppose that mh/ originally belonged to the infinitive,
and afterwards came to negative the whole expression. See the examples
in 734.

§739

（Present Wishes in Homer.) In
Homer a present unattained wish may be expressed by the present

*ei) ga\r e)gw\n ou(/tw
ge *dio\s pa/is ai)gio/xoio ei)/hn h)/mata pa/nta, te/koi de/ me
