you.]

If it is thought that the limited number of cases of
independent mh/ with the
subjunctive not implying apprehension do not justify the assumptions
which have been based on them, it is easy to see how the change from the
denial of an apprehension to the denial of a suspicion might have taken
place within the ou) mh/
construction itself. If we suppose such expressions as ou) mh\ lhfqw= and ou) mh/ ti/s se u(bri/sh| to
have been established as the negatives of mh\ lhfqw=, I fear I
may be caught, and mh/
ti/s se u(bri/sh|, I fear some one
may insult you, they must soon have fallen out of this
relation to the parent forms, and have been felt in use to be mere
future negative assertions, so that they could not long be restricted to
sentences in which apprehension was implied. Thus, ou) mh\ nau=s a)formi/sh| xqono/s would soon
become as natural to those who used these forms as the older ou) mh/ ti/s se u(bri/sh|.
According to this view, ou)
mh/ with the subjunctive would come into the language in the
sense of a denial of an apprehension, which is essentially the same
general sense as that supposed by the theory of an ellipsis of de/os e)sti/n. But there is a
great advantage in dispensing with this troublesome and improbable
ellipsis, and deriving the meaning from the sentence as it stands. There
is surely no more ground for assuming this ellipsis here than in the
independent subjunctive with mh/, which is an older construction than the dependent
subjunctive with mh/. And if
we accept mh/ ti/s se
u(bri/sh| as a complete construction, without the help of de/os e)sti/n, it is absurd to
invent an ellipsis to explain ou)
mh/ ti/s se u(bri/sh| as a shorter form for ou) de/os e)sti\ mh/ ti/s se
u(bri/sh|. In fact, dispensing with this ellipsis removes the
most fatal objection to the view of the sentence on which the old theory
was based.

In whichever of the two ways above suggested the subjunctive
with ou) mh/ came to express
a simple future denial, it was only natural that the Attic Greek should
soon begin to use the future indicative in place of the subjunctive in
the same sense. Thus we have in

SOPH. El. 1052,

ou)/ soi mh\ meqe/yomai/
pote
, and in

AR. Ran.
508,

ou) mh/ s' e)gw\
perio/yomai
, both expressing denial. At this stage all recollection of the
original clause with mh/ and
the subjunctive must have been lost, as there was no corresponding
clause with mh/ and the
future indicative in common use, of which ou) mh/ with the future could be the
negative. A most striking proof of the entire loss of this tradition is
given by examples of indirect quotation of ou) mh/ with the future. In
SOPH. Ph. 611
we have ta/ t' a)/lla ta/nt'
e)qe/spisen, kai\ ta)pi\ *troi/as pe/rgam' w(s ou) mh/ pote
pe/rsoien ei) mh\ to/nde a)/gointo, the direct form being
ou) mh/ pote pe/rsete e)a\n mh\
to/nde a)/ghsqe. In

XEN. Hell.
i. 6, 32,

ei)=pen o(/ti h( *spa/rth
ou)de\n mh\ ka/kion oi)kiei=tai au)tou= a)poqano/ntos
, the future indicative is retained in an otherwise similar
construction. In
EUR. Ph. 1590, we find ei)=pe *teiresi/as ou) mh/ pote, sou= th/nde gh=n oi)kou=ntos, eu)=
pra/cein to/lin, representing ou) mh/ pote eu)= pra/cei. We could not
explain ou) mh\ pra/cein as
an independent expression on any theory, either with or without an
ellipsis. Such forms show the advanced stage within the construction of
ou) mh/ had reached.
(See § 296.)

We find in the Roman comic poets a few cases of neque with haud in the same clause, forming a
single negative. Such are

PLAUT. Bacch.
1037,

Neque
ego haud committam ut, si mid
peccatum siet, fecisse dicas de mea sententia
; and

TER. Andr. 205,

Neque
tu haud dices tibi non
praedictum
. Neque haud may
fairly be supposed to be a translation of ou)de\ mh/ in a Greek original. If it is, it
shows that the Roman poet understood ou) mh/ with the subjunctive or the future indicative as a
simple expression of denial.

When ou) mh/ with
the future indicative had been established as a regular form of future
denial, the second person singular probably began to be used as a form
of prohibition. As the future could be used in positive commands in an
imperative sense, as in

pa/ntws de\ tou=to dra/seis,

but by all means do this,

AR. Nub.
1352
, it could also take the simple ou) in prohibitions, as in

xeiri\ d' ou)yau/seis pote,

you shall not touch me with your hand, [note: or do not touch
me] .

EUR. Med.
1320.
(See §
69.) The dramatists soon introduced the form with ou) mh/ into such prohibitions,
generally with the future indicative, but occasionally with the more
primitive subjunctive. Thus ou) mh\
katabh/sei had the sense of do not
come down, derived from you shall not
come down, as ou)
yau/seis (above) from meaning you
shall not touch came to mean do not
touch. One of the strongest objections to the older views of
the forms with ou) mh/ is
that they generally require a distinct explanation of this prohibitory
construction. Elmsley's theory of a question with two negatives,
explaining ou) mh\
katabh/sei; as will you NOT NOT come down? hence do not come down, was stated in the Quarterly Review for June 1812, and in his
note to
EUR. Med.
1120 (1151 Dind.). Many who do not adopt Elmsley's theory in
full still accept the interrogative form, and these sentences are now
generally printed as questions. Long before Elmsley, the famous

Canon Davesianus had proscribed all sigmatic aorist
subjunctives with ou) mh/ as
well as with o(/pws mh/.
This edict removed nearly or quite all the troublesome subjunctives that
would have opposed Elmsley's view, and left only the future indicative
in his doubly-negatived questions, which of course required an
indicative. This again set up an artificial distinction in form between
the prohibitory construction allowing only the future indicative, and
the other construction allowing both subjunctive and future indicative.

But it has been more and more evident in later years that
this distinction in form between the two constructions cannot be
maintained. It was seen by Brunck, before Elmsley's interrogative theory
appeared, that it would be absurd to distinguish sentences like

tau=ta ou) mh/ pot' e)s th\n
*sku=ron e)kpleu/sh|s e)/xwn

you shall never sail away to Scyros with
these arms,

SOPH. Ph.
381
, from

ou) mh\ katabh/sei

you shall not come down,

AR. Vesp.
397
. He therefore wrote e)kpleu/seis in the former, with the note
soloece vulgo legitur e)kpleu/sh|s. But e)kpleu/seis proved to be even
a greater solecism than e)kpleu/sh|s was thought to be, for the only classic future of
ple/w is the middle
pleu/somai or pleusou=mai, and e)kpleu/sei will not suit the
verse. So e)kpleu/sh|s had
to be restored. Again, while almost all the sentences containing a
prohibition with ou) mh/,
followed by a positive command with a)lla/ or de/,
could admit of Elmsley's punctuation and interpretation,—as

ou) mh\ lalh/seis a)ll'
a)kolouqh/seis e)moi/;

AR. Nub.
505
, explained as won't you not talk nonsense
and follow me? — another passage of the Clouds
resisted both of these and also the prescribed form. In
296, the
Mss. have ou) mh\ skw/yh|s mhde\
poih/sh|s a(/per oi( trugodai/mones ou(=toi: a)ll'
eu)fh/mei. Brunck emended this without hesitation to ou) mh\ skw/yeis mhde\
poih/seis, with the note

soloece vulgo skw/yh|s . . .
poih/sh|s. But there was no place for
Elmsley's interrogative mark, which could not stand after the
imperative, and could not be inserted after ou(=toi without implying that the other
sentences (like
AR. Nub. 505 above) were wrongly punctuated. The emendation
skw/yeis was as
unfortunate as e)kpleu/seis,
as the future of skw/ptw is
skw/yomai, not skw/yw, so that a further
emendation to skw/yei was
needed. In this battered condition, and with no interrogative mark to
help the interpretation, the passage usually appears, even in the latest
editions. (See §§ 298, 300, 301.) So long as it is proposed to explain these
prohibitions and the ordinary denials with ou) mh/ on entirely different theories, with
nothing common to the two constructions, it may not seem unreasonable to
force a few examples like
AR. Nub. 296 and
367 into conformity with the
general usage. But on any theory which makes no distinction in
construction between the prohibitions and the other negative expressions
of denial or refusal (for example, between ou) mh\ e)kpleu/sh|s, you shall not sail away, and ou) mh\ katabh/sei, do not come down, i.e. you shall not
come down), there is no more reason for objecting to ou) mh\ skw/yh|s than to ou) mh\ e)kpleu/sh|s. An
occasional subjunctive, like ou) mh\
skw/yh|s or ou) mh\
lhrh/sh|s, is indeed no more than we should naturally expect
in a construction which had its origin in the subjunctive. In such
expressions, further, the analogy of the equivalent mh\ skw/yh|s and mh\ lhrh/sh|s would tend to make the aorist
subjunctive unobjectionable and perfectly natural. A reference to the
list of passages quoted on page 390 will show the inconsistencies into
which every one must fall who attempts to explain the prohibitions and
the clauses of denial on different theories. We cannot separate ou) mh\ skw/yh|s from ou) mh\ e)kpleu/sh|s in
construction, nor the latter from ou) mh\ pa/qh|s, nor this again from ou) mh/ tis u(bri/sh|, on any consistent
principle of interpretation. [note: For a further discussion of the form
of the sentences with ou)
mh/, in connexion with that of clauses with o(/pws and with the Canon
Davesianus, see Trans. of the Phil.
Assoc. for 1869-70, pp. 46-55.]

Sentences of one class have been claimed as decisive
witnesses in favour of the interrogative theory. They are represented by

ou) qa=sson oi)/seis, mhd'
a)pisth/seis e)moi/;

will you not more quickly extend it (your
hand), and not distrust me?

SOPH. Tr.
1183.
These are undoubted questions, but there is no construction with
ou) mh/ in them. They
consist of one question with ou), implying an affirmative answer, will you not extend your hand? and another with mh/, implying a negative
answer, and you will not distrust me, will
you? The compound of the two has the general sense expressed in
the first translation above. (See § 299 and the examples.)

In conclusion, we may sum up the result of the investigation
as follows. The original construction of ou) mh/ with the subjunctive was developed
as a negative form of the independent subjunctive with mh/, which had already become
an expression of apprehension with desire to avert its object, even if
it had not passed into the stage of a cautious assertion; in either
case, the real negative force of mh/ was in abeyance. The aorist subjunctive is the most common
form here, the present being less frequent. This form of future denial
next admitted the future indicative in the same sense as the
subjunctive. The second person singular of this future with ou) mh/ was used by the
dramatists as a prohibition, without abandoning the sense which the
future can always have in both positive and negative commands. In these
prohibitions the future indicative, in which they had their origin, is
generally used; but the subjunctive occasionally occurs, being analogous
to the ordinary aorist subjunctive with mh/ in prohibitions; e.g. mh\ skw/yh|s supporting ou) mh\ skw/yh|s. [note: Since this paper
was written, I have seen that Kvičala, in two articles on
ou) mh/ in the
Zeitschrift für die
oesterreichischen Gymnasien for 1856, proposed an
explanation of ou) mh/
with the subjunctive, which at one important point came very near
the view now presented. He states two (apparently theoretical)
meanings which he supposes mh\
qa/nh|s to have had at some period (zwei Bedeutungsentwickelungen): one,

Du wirst doch wol am
Ende, trotzdem dass ich es abzuwehren suche, sterben;
the other,
Ich
fürchte, dass du doch wol (trotz meiner Abwehr) sterben
werdest. By prefixing ou) to mh\ qa/nh|s in these meanings, he
arrives at two uses of ou)
mh/ with the subjunctive. The second meaning comes so near
the independent subjunctive with mh/ in Homer, that it is surprising that neither this
nor the equally important mh/ in Plato is mentioned. But no use is made of the
advantage here gained in explaining ou) mh/ with the future indicative,
either in prohibitions or in denials. The prohibitions are made
interrogative, ou) mh\ dusmenh\s
e)/sei; being explained as
Nicht wahr?—du wirst doch nicht
feindselig seyn? The future of denial is
explained simply as developed from the interrogative future, as a
form of reply to this, by leaving out the interrogative
element.]

## Xenophon's Peculiar use of w(s, w(s a)/n, and o(/pws a)/n in Final and Object Clauses.

## In Final Clauses.

I. (*(ws, and
w(s a)/n.) 1. It is well
known that Xenophon is almost the only writer of Attic prose who uses
w(s freely in the final
constructions. Weber's statistics (p. 398) show that while w(s is the favourite final
particle in tragedy, it is hardly found in Aristophanes, Thucydides,
Plato, and the Orators. Xenophon forms a strange exception to the prose
usage, having w(s or w(s a)/n in 91 of his pure
final clauses. There is nothing peculiar in his use of final w(s with either subjunctive or
optative, as it merely takes the place of another final particle.

2. In his use of w(s
a)/n in final clauses, however, several peculiarities appear,
which show that Xenophon felt the original force of w(s as a relative adverb of manner (§ 312). The
following examples occur. [note: See Weber, p. 224, where the examples of the optative
with w(s a)/n are also
given. Weber cites
Cyr. viii. 3. 2 as an example of the
subjunctive; but this section has w(s a)\n e)caggei/lh| as a relative
clause, but no final clause. I have added
Cyr. vii.
5. 81 and
Eques. ix. 3 to the examples of the
optative given by Weber.]

II. (*(/opws.)
Xenophon's favourite final particle is o(/pws, but there is nothing peculiar in his
use of it in pure final clauses with either subjunctive or optative. He
further uses o(/pws a)/n
with the subjunctive like other Attic writers (see examples in § 328).

With the optative he uses o(/pws a)/n in four cases with a distinct final and an
equally distinct potential force. These examples are quoted in § 330. The
only other case is
THUC. vii. 65.

## In Object Clauses after Verbs of Striving etc.

Xenophon is more peculiar in his use of w(s, w(s a)/n, and o(/pws a)/n in these clauses than in pure
final clauses. Here he generally uses o(/pws with the future indicative,
subjunctive, and optative, and occasionally o(/pws a)/n with the subjunctive, like other
Attic writers (see examples in §§ 339 and 348). But he distinctly violates
Attic usage by having w(s
(in the sense of o(/pws）
with both subjunctive and future indicative, and with the present,
aorist, and future optative; also w(s a)/n with both subjunctive and optative and o(/pws a)/n with the optative;
and further by allowing the optative with w(s a)/n and o(/pws a)/n to follow both primary and
secondary tenses. His use of w(s
a)/n and o(/pws
a)/n with the optative, especially after primary tenses, shows
strongly the original relative and interrogative force of w(s and o(/pws.

[section 4]

## On some Disputed Points in the Construction of e)/dei, xrh=n, etc. with the
Infinitive. [note: Many parts of this paper are identical with the article with the same
title in the Harvard Studies in Classical Philology, vol. i. pp.
77-88.]

## Supplement to §§ 415-423.

THE familiar construction by which e)/dei, xrh=n or e)xrh=n, ei)ko\s h)=n, prosh=ken, e)ch=n, and
other imperfects denoting obligation, propriety,
or possibility, are used with the infinitive in
an idiomatic sense, the whole expression becoming a form of potential
indicative, and generally implying the opposite of the action or the
negation of the infinitive, has already been explained in §§ 415-423. Some
additional remarks, however, seem necessary, to guard against prevailing
misapprehensions.

The important distinction between this idiomatic construction and
the use of these imperfects as ordinary past tenses (§ 417) is generally indicated
only by the context, and not by the words themselves. It may even be
doubtful in some cases which meaning is intended. Thus, in

DEM. xviii. 190,

ti/ to\n su/mboulon e)xrh=n poiei=n;
ou) . . . e(le/sqai;
nothing in the words shows whether the action of e(le/sqai is real or not; but the following
tou=to toi/nun e)poi/hsa
shows that the questions refer merely to a past duty which the speaker
actually performed. Indeed, the idiomatic use of e)/dei etc. with the infinitive may be found in
the same sentence with the ordinary use of these imperfects as past tenses
without reference to any condition. A familiar case is in the New Testament,

MATTH. xxiii. 23,

tau=ta de\ e)/dei poih=sai ka)kei=na
mh\ a)fei=nai
, these [note: (the weightier matters of the
law)] ought ye to have done, and yet not to have left the others
[note: (taking tithes)] undone. This is equivalent to two
sentences, tau=ta e)/dei u(ma=s
poih=sai, ye ought to have done these
(which ye did not do), and e)kei=na
e)/dei u(ma=s mh\ a)fei=nai, ye were
right in not leaving those undone (which ye did not leave
undone). We have a decisive proof of the idiomatic use when the present
infinitive with e)/dei etc.
refers to present time, as when xrh=n se
tou=to poiei=n means you ought to be
doing this (but are not); for these words without the potential
force could mean only it was (once) your duty to do
this. This use of a past tense to express present time, which is
found in Greek, Latin, and English (§ 417), is an important characteristic of this
idiom.

It is generally laid down as an absolute rule that in this idiom
the opposite of the infinitive is always
implied. See Krüger, § 53, 2, 7, where the usual formula is
given, that with e)/dei tou=to
gi/gnesqai we must understand a)ll' ou) gi/gnetai, but with e)/dei a)\n tou=to gi/gnesqai we
must understand a)ll' ou) dei=.
This principle was first formulated, I believe, by G. Hermann. [note: See Hermann, de Particula *)/an, i. 12. In discussing

SOPH. Elec.
1505,

xrh=n d' eu)qu\s ei)=nai th/nde
toi=s pa=sin di/khn
, Hermann says: *xrh=n dicit, quia
oportere indicat sine condicione: nec potest opponi, a)ll' ou) xrh/: nam si
oportet, quomodo potest non oportere? At non omnia fiunt, quae
oportebat. Itaque quod opponere potes, aliud est: a)ll' ou)k
e)/sti. The
opposite implied in a
negative expression of this kind (even when the negation belongs to the
leading verb) is an affirmative. Thus ou) prosh=ken e)lqei=n, he ought not to have gone, implies a)ll' h)=lqen, as e)/dei tou/tous mh\ zh=n
implies a)lla\
zw=sin.] It covers nearly all the ordinary cases, and has
generally been found to be a convenient working rule, though many passages
show that it is not of universal application. The following three classes of
examples show the need of a more flexible formula.

(1) In the following cases the opposite of the leading verb is
implied far more than that of the infinitive, the action of the latter in
the first case being emphatically affirmed:—

HDT. i. 39

,

(2) In concessive sentences introduced by kai\ ei), even
if, ou)d' ei), not even if, or ei), although,
which contain unreal conditions, the action or negation of the apodosis must
be distinctly affirmed (§
412, 3). Here, therefore, the common formula cannot be applied.

See
ISOC.

i.e. even if you had not all mankind with

It is well known that the imperfects in question (without a)/n) can be used with the
infinitive in two ways, — (a) alone, with no protasis expressed or
implied except the condition which is contained in the expression itself, as

e)nh=n ai)tia/sasqai

could mean only he could not maintain a suit
as he does; that is, it would mean nothing without a protasis.

truth.）

When these potential expressions without a)/n stand alone, they always imply the opposite
of the action or the negation of the infinitive; so that ei)ko\s h)=n se tou=to paqei=n by itself can
mean only you would properly have suffered
this (but you did not). This is necessary because the equivalent of
this form, tou=to a)\n e)/paqes ei) to\
ei)ko\s e)/paqes, always involves ou)k e)/paqes tou=to, since tou=to and to\ ei)ko/s are here made identical, and to\ ei)ko\s e)/paqes is denied. When, however,
one of these expressions is made the apodosis of an unreal condition
external to itself, it may be so modified by the new condition as no longer
to imply the opposite of the infinitive as before. This is the case with the
four examples under (1), in which we certainly do not find ou) poie/eis, a)/llo le/gei kai\
sumbouleu/ei, ou)k h)|tia/sato, and ou)k h)ra/sqhs implied in the form of
expression. The apparent paradox here is explained by the principle stated
in § 511, that
when several protases, not co-ordinate, belong to the same sentence, one
always contains the leading condition, to which the rest of the sentence
(including the other conditions) forms the conclusion; and when this leading
condition is unreal, it makes all subordinate past or present conditions
also unreal, so far as the supposed case is concerned, without regard to
their own nature. A sentence like this, If you had been
an Athenian, you would have been laughed at if you had talked as you
did, shows the principle clearly. This has become the relation of the
unreal protasis involved in ei)ko\s h)=n
se tou=to paqei=n, when this expression is made the apodosis of
a new unreal condition. Thus, when xrh=n
se poie/ein in
HDT. i. 39, which by itself could admit only an unreal object,
follows ei) u(po\ o)do/ntos ei)=pe
teleuth/sein me, even ta\
poie/eis can be its object, and the whole can mean if the dream had said I was to perish by a tooth, you
would do what you now do if you did what was right. The new chief
protasis that has come in has changed the whole relation of the old implied
protasis to the sentence as a whole.

It is often difficult to express in English the exact force of
these expressions, even when no external protasis is added, and the opposite
of the infinitive (not that of the leading verb) is therefore implied. Thus,
a common translation of

DEM. xviii. 248,

ou)d' a)gnwmonh=sai/ ti qaumasto\n
h)=n tou\s pollou\s pro\s e)me/
, it would have been no wonder if the mass of
the people had been somewhat unmindful of me (Westermann
translates entschuldbar gewesen wä
re), would seem to require h)=n a)/n. But the strength of the apodosis lies
in the infinitive, and the meaning (fully developed) is, the mass of the people might have been somewhat
unmindful of me (h)gnwmo/nhsan a)/n ti) without doing
anything wonderful (i.e. if they had done
a very natural thing). With qaumasto\n a)\n h)=n there would have been an undue emphasis
thrown upon qaumasto/n. In

PLAT. Rep. 474 D,

a)/llw| e)/prepen le/gein a(\
le/geis
is equivalent to a)/llos e)/legen
a)\n prepo/ntws a(\ le/geis, another
would becomingly say what you say, the opposite of le/gein being implied. *)/eprepen a)\n le/gein would have
caused a change of emphasis, but would have substantially the same general
meaning, it would have been becoming for another to say
what you say. See also
DEM. xviii. 16,
xlv. 69, and
PLAT. Euthyd. 304 D, quoted in § 419; and the
discussion of
EUR. Med.
490 in §
422, 1.

We have seen that we cannot make the denial of the action of the
infinitive an absolute test of the proper use of the form without a)/n where there is an external
protasis added to the condition implied in the expression itself. The
examples last quoted show that we cannot make the denial of the leading verb
an absolute test of the proper use of the form with a)/n. In fact, this idiom is too flexible and
too dependent on the momentary feeling of the speaker or writer to subject
itself to any such strict rules as are usually forced upon it. The following
rules seem to me to be as exact as the Greek usage warrants. [note: When an external
protasis is added, there is no necessity for any denial of the action of
the apodosis at all (see § 412). But this denial, though not essential, is
generally implied in the apodosis of an unreal condition, and the
apodosis (as a whole) happens to be denied in all the cases of the
construction of e)/dei etc.
with the infinitive which are discussed here. No notice is taken,
therefore, of the principle of § 412 in this discussion.]

1. The form without a)/n is used when the infinitive is the principal word, on which
the chief force of the expression falls, while the leading verb is an
auxiliary which we can express by ought, might,
could, or by an adverb.

2. On the other hand, when the chief force falls on the
necessity, propriety, or possibility of the act, and not on the act itself,
the leading verb has a)/n, like
any other imperfect in a similar apodosis.

Examples of the form with a)/n are generally regular. See those quoted in § 423. [note: See La Roche on a)/n bei e)/dei
und e)ch=n in
the Zeitschrift für die
oesterreichischen Gymnasien for 1876, pp. 588-591. He
professes to give all the cases; but his twenty-one examples of e)/dei a)/n include eleven in
which e)/dei has the
genitive of a noun and no infinitive. Omitting these, we have only ten
of e)/dei a)/n with the
infinitive:
THUC. i.
74,
LYS. Frag. 56
(88 Scheibe);
ISOC.
XV. 17;
ISAE. iv. 4;
DEM. iv. 1;
PLAT. Rep. 328 C,
Theaet. 169
E,
Gorg.
514 A,
Alc. i. 119 B;
DEM. lvii. 47 (only the last
three affirmative); with four of e)ch=n a)/n:
LYS. iv. 13, Frag. 47 (79 Scheibe);
ISAE. X. 13;

DEM. xxiv.
146. He finds xrh=n
a)/n only in
LYS. xii. 48, where he proposes to omit a)/n, overlooking xrh=n a)\n prosdokh=sai in
DEM. xviii. 195.
Both of these passages are discussed below, pp. 409, 410.] A
standard case is

DEM. iv. 1,

ei) ta\ de/onta ou(=toi
sunebou/leusan, ou)de\n a)\n u(ma=s nu=n e)/dei bouleu/esqai
, if these had given you the necessary advice,
there would be no need of your deliberating now. Here, as in all
the ten examples of e)/dei a)/n
quoted by La Roche, we find e)/dei
a)/n in its meaning there would be (or would
have been) need, whereas in the form without a)/n we generally have e)/dei in the sense of ought, expressing obligation and not
necessity. Of course, the idea of necessity
is incompatible with that of an act not done. If La Roche's statistics are
complete here, we see that the Greeks almost always expressed obligation or
propriety, and generally expressed possibility, by the form without a)/n, reserving e)/dei a)/n for the idea of necessity, and
e)ch=n a)/n for a few cases
in which the idea of possibility was to be made specially emphatic.

It is not surprising, under these circumstances, that the form
without a)/n should often be
used where we are at first inclined to think a)/n is required. It must be remembered that the
real apodosis here is not the central infinitive alone, but this infinitive
modified by the idea of obligation, propriety, or possibility in the leading
verb, that is, conditioned by the implied protasis which the expression
includes (see §
420). This modification may be so slight as to leave the infinitive
the only important word in the apodosis; in this case the opposite of the
infinitive is generally implied, as it always is when no protasis is added:
thus,

EUR. Med. 520,

xrh=n s', ei)/per h)=sqa mh\ kako\s,
pei/santa/ me gamei=n ga/mon to/nde
, implies a)ll' ou)k e)ga/meis
pei/sas me. It may be so great as to make the idea of obligation
etc. a prominent factor in the apodosis, still stopping short of the point
at which this favourite Greek idiom was abandoned and an ordinary apodosis
with a)/n was substituted in its
place. The Greeks preferred the form without a)/n almost always where we can express the
apodosis by the verb of the infinitive with ought,
might, or could, or with an adverb,
although we sometimes find it hard to express the combined idea in English
without giving undue force to the leading verb. Sometimes, when the idea of
obligation, propriety, or possibility is specially prominent in the
apodosis, although no a)/n is
used, the opposite that is suggested combines this idea with that of the
infinitive. This is the case with the examples in (1), in which the distinction between
the two forms is very slight and of little practical account. In
HDT. i. 39, the
apodosis is you would then properly do what you now
do (or you would then, if you did what
you ought, do what you now do), implying now you do not do this properly. With xrh=n a)/n it would have been it would then be your duty to do what you now
do, the chief force being transferred from the act to the duty or
necessity. Still, this change might have been made without otherwise
affecting the sense. In
DEM.
ix. 6, the apodosis is in that case the
speaker would properly talk of nothing else than this (implying
now he may properly talk of another matter);
whereas with e)/dei a)/n it

anything else, with greater emphasis on the e)/dei and with a change of meaning. In

DEM. xxiii. 37,

means he might then possibly have accused

it was; with e)nh=n

EUR. Med. 490. Likewise, in

e)qauma/zomen a)ci/ws, with the opposite implied, now we do wonder at him properly (nu=n qauma/zomen a)ci/ws). This
combination of two ideas in an apodosis of this kind is analogous to that
which we often find in an ordinary apodosis with a)/n; thus, in

ISOC. vi. 87,

ou)x ou(/tw d' a)\n proqu/mws e)pi\

ou(/tw proqu/mws.

A striking illustration of the modification of the infinitive in
an apodosis of this kind by the force of the leading verb may be seen in the
examples under (3). Here
in concessive sentences, in which the apodosis must be affirmed, we find the
action of the infinitives denied. This shows that the infinitive alone is
not the real apodosis. In
SOPH. OT 255, the actual apodosis is
you
would not properly leave the guilt unpurged (implying you do not properly leave it). In

they
would deservedly have received, = e)/tuxon a)\n a)ci/ws (implying that it was only
undeservedly that they failed to receive the reward). The remarks that have been made
above apply also to the concessive sentences in (2), in which nothing in the apodosis is
denied. Here, too, the form with a)/n might have been used by transferring the force of the
expression from the infinitive to the leading verb.

It has been seen that e)/dei

It remains to discuss two passages in which xrh=n a)/n occurs, with a view to La Roche's
disbelief in the existence of this form (see footnote 2, p. 407). In
DEM. xviii. 195, we
have xrh=n and xrh=n a)/n in close succession,
with no essential change in meaning except the difference in emphasis above
mentioned. The sentence is: ei) meta\
*qhbai/wn h(mi=n a)gwnizome/nois ou(/tws ei(/marto pra=cai, ti/ xrh=n
prosdoka=n ei) mhde\ tou/tous e)/sxomen summa/xous; . . . kai\ ei) nu=n
triw=n h(merw=n a)po\ th=s *)attikh=s o(do\n th=s ma/xhs genome/nhs

journey from Attica, what should we have had to expect (which we did not
really have to expect) if this calamity had occurred within our own
country? Here the unreal supposition of not having secured the
Thebans as allies, or (its probable consequence) the battle of Chaeronea
having been fought in Attica, suits either form of apodosis, ti/ xrh=n prosdoka=n; or ti/ a)\n xrh=n prosdokh=sai; the
expectation itself in the former case, and the necessity for the expectation
in the latter, being specially emphasised. It is hard to believe that the
orator felt any important change in the general force of his question when
he added a)/n in the second

In

lawlessness in office, and, next, to come before the Senate as an

absurd to suppose that a)ll'
e)xrh=n is implied in the sense that E. had a
right to be lawless in office (
er durfte
parano/mws a)/rxein）
because he was not honest. What is implied is rather a)ll' ou)k e)xrh=n mh\ parano/mws a)/rxein, i.e.
not being an honest man, he did not have to

understand without absurdity. The passage, like so many sentences of this
class, is simply an argument to prove that E. was not honest. If he had been honest (it is said), he would have had to do certain things (which, it
is implied, all honest men do); but he did not do
these (as is stated, ei)s th\n
a)rxh\n katasta\s a)gaqou= me\n ou)deno\s mete/sxen, a)/llwn de\
pollw=n); therefore he was not honest.
There is a slight slip in showing (in the words last quoted) that he did not do the things in question, and not that
he did not have to do them; so that of the
two constructions, xrh=n in 32
and e)xrh=n a)/n in 48, the
former is more strictly logical. This use of e)xrh=n a)/n is the counterpart of that of
xrh=n, e)/dei, e)nh=n, and
qaumasto\n h)=n in the

The Latin follows precisely the same principle as the Greek in
the use of such imperfects as debebat,
licebat (= xrh=n,
e)ch=n), and deberet,
liceret (= xrh=n a)/n, e)ch=n
a)/n), with reference to present time. But when such expressions
are past, the Latin uses debuit or debuerat
in the sense of xrh=n, and
debuisset for xrh=n a)/n, both with the present
infinitive; while the Greek keeps the imperfect in all cases. See

CIC. Phil. ii. 99,

Quem patris loco, si ulla in te pietas
esset, colere debebas
(= xrh=n se filei=n),
you ought to love (but you do not); and

Cluent. 18,

Cluentio ignoscere debebitis quod haec
a me dici patiatur; mihi ignoscere non
deberes si tacerem
(= ou) a)/n se e)moi\
suggignw/skein xrh=n ei) e)si/gwn), it

former case the emphasis falls on colere; in the latter on non deberes, which is in strong antithesis to debebitis. See also

CIC. Verr. ii.
5, 50:

Qui ex foedere ipso navem vel usque ad
Oceanum, si imperassemus, mittere
debuerunt, ei, ne in freto ante sua tecta et domos
navigarent, . . . pretio abs te ius foederis et imperii condicionem

of mittere, but rather
something like what is implied in the examples in (1), like they did not have to send.
Mittere debuissent (e)/dei a)\n pe/myai) would mean
they would have been bound to send. In
Latin, as in Greek and English, the peculiar force of the past tense of the
indicative with the infinitive is purely idiomatic.

## Deliberative Constructions

IN a paper on The Extent of the

3. A further extension of the deliberative usage leads to the
subjunctive and optative in clauses introduced by true relatives with
distinct antecedents, when these depend on expressions implying doubt,
perplexity, or ignorance. See examples in § 572, 2. Thus, in ou) ga\r a)/llon oi)=d' o(/tw|

The former is the result of a simple evolution, by which a relative

final force is felt in the expression comes from the intimate relation
